shanti.1: Om. That (the unseen Brahman) is whole; this (the seen world) is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth. When the whole is taken from the whole, the whole alone remains. Om, peace, peace, peace.

The Brahman is infinite, so the world that comes from it takes nothing away from it. Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature (ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika).
1.1.1: The dawn, truly, is the head of the horse fit for sacrifice. The sun is its eye, the wind its prāṇa (the vital breath), the fire Vaiśvānara its open mouth, and the year the body of the horse fit for sacrifice. The sky is its back, the mid-region its belly, the earth the ground for its feet, the quarters its two flanks, the intermediate quarters its ribs, the seasons its limbs, the months and half-months its joints, days and nights its feet, the stars its bones, the clouds its flesh; the sands are the half-digested food in its stomach, the rivers its veins, the mountains its liver and lungs, the herbs and trees its hairs; the rising sun is its front half, the setting sun its hind half; when it yawns, that is the lightning; when it shakes itself, that is the thunder; when it makes water, that is the rain; sound itself is its voice. ॥1.1.1॥
Śaṅkara reads this as a meditation for the horse sacrifice: the horse is seen as Prajāpati, with time, the worlds and the gods laid on its limbs; the dawn is the hour before sunrise (brāhma muhūrta).
1.1.2: The day arose before the horse as the mahiman, the sacrificial cup of that name; its place is the eastern sea. The night arose behind it as the mahiman; its place is the western sea. These two mahimans came into being on either side of the horse. As haya it carried the gods, as vājin the gandharvas, as arvan the demons (asuras), as aśva men. The sea alone is its bond, that in which it is bound; the sea is its source. ॥1.1.2॥
Śaṅkara takes the sea here as the supreme Self, or as the sea itself, known as the horse's birthplace. Others take bandhu as kin.
1.2.1: In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by Death, by hunger, for hunger is death. He made the mind, thinking: Let me have a self (a mind). He moved about, worshipping. As he worshipped, the waters were born. He thought: As I worshipped, ka (water) truly came to me. That is why the arka (the sacrificial fire) is called arka. Ka, water or joy, truly comes to him who knows thus why the arka is called arka. ॥1.2.1॥
1.2.2: The waters, truly, are the arka. What was the cream (śara) on the waters became solid. That became the earth. When it had been made, he (Death) grew weary. From him, wearied and heated, his radiance, his essence, came forth as fire. ॥1.2.2॥
1.2.3: He divided himself threefold: the sun as a third, the air as a third (and fire as a third). This prāṇa, the vital breath, is divided threefold. The east is its head, and that quarter and that (the north-east and the south-east) its forelegs; the west is its tail, and that and that (the north-west and the south-west) its hind legs; the south and the north its two flanks; the sky its back, the mid-region its belly, this (earth) its chest. It rests on the waters. He who knows thus finds a firm footing wherever he goes. ॥1.2.3॥
1.2.4: He desired: Let a second self (a body) be born to me. He, Death, who is hunger, united with speech through the mind. The seed that was there became the year. Before that there was no year. He bore him for as long as a year lasts, and after that long a time he brought him forth. Death opened his mouth at the newborn one (to eat him). He cried bhāṇ; that became speech. ॥1.2.4॥
Śaṅkara takes speech here as the threefold Veda: with the mind, Death reviewed the order of creation it lays down.
1.2.5: He thought: If I kill him, I shall make less food (for myself). With that speech and that self (the mind) he brought forth all this, whatever there is: the Ṛks, the Yajuses, the Sāmans, the metres, the sacrifices, the creatures, the animals. Whatever he brought forth, he resolved to eat. He eats (atti) all: that is why Aditi is called Aditi. He who knows thus why Aditi is called Aditi becomes the eater of all this, and all becomes his food. ॥1.2.5॥
1.2.6: He desired: Let me sacrifice again, with a greater sacrifice. He toiled; he practised austerity (tapas). From him, wearied and heated, glory and vigour went out. The prāṇas (the organs) are glory and vigour. When the prāṇas had gone out, the body began to swell. Yet his mind was in that very body. ॥1.2.6॥
1.2.7: He desired: May this (body) of mine be fit for sacrifice, and through it may I have a body. Then it became a horse (aśva), because it had swollen (aśvat); it had become fit for sacrifice (medhya). That is why the horse sacrifice is called aśvamedha. He alone truly knows the aśvamedha who knows it thus. He thought of it as let loose, unconfined. After a year he sacrificed it to himself. The other animals he handed over to the gods. That is why (the priests) sacrifice to Prajāpati the consecrated horse that belongs to all the gods. He who shines there (the sun) is indeed the aśvamedha; the year is his body. This fire is the arka; these worlds are its bodies. These two are the arka and the aśvamedha. Yet they become one deity again, Death alone. (He who knows this) conquers repeated death; death does not reach him; death becomes his self; he becomes one of these deities. ॥1.2.7॥
1.3.1: Prajāpati's offspring were of two kinds: the gods and the demons. Of them the gods were the fewer, the demons the more. They vied with one another for these worlds. The gods said: Come, let us surpass the demons in the sacrifice by means of the udgītha, the chant of the Sāman. ॥1.3.1॥
Śaṅkara takes the gods and the demons as Prajāpati's own senses, speech and the rest: gods when shaped by scripture, demons when moved by natural impulse alone.
1.3.2: They said to speech: Chant the udgītha for us. Speech said: So be it. Speech chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in speech it won for the gods by its chanting; its speaking well it kept for itself. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one speaks, that is the evil. ॥1.3.2॥
1.3.3: Then they said to prāṇa, the vital breath (here the breath by which one smells): Chant the udgītha for us. Prāṇa said: So be it. Prāṇa chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in prāṇa it won for the gods by its chanting; its smelling well it kept for itself. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one smells, that is the evil. ॥1.3.3॥
1.3.4: Then they said to the eye: Chant the udgītha for us. The eye said: So be it. The eye chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the eye it won for the gods by its chanting; its seeing well it kept for itself. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one sees, that is the evil. ॥1.3.4॥
1.3.5: Then they said to the ear: Chant the udgītha for us. The ear said: So be it. The ear chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the ear it won for the gods by its chanting; its hearing well it kept for itself. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one hears, that is the evil. ॥1.3.5॥
1.3.6: Then they said to the mind: Chant the udgītha for us. The mind said: So be it. The mind chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the mind it won for the gods by its chanting; its thinking well it kept for itself. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one thinks, that is the evil. So indeed they brought evils upon these deities; so they pierced them with evil. ॥1.3.6॥
1.3.7: Then they said to this prāṇa in the mouth: Chant the udgītha for us. Prāṇa said: So be it. This prāṇa chanted for them. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us. They rushed at it and sought to pierce it with evil. As a clod of earth would be shattered on striking a stone, so they were shattered, scattered in all directions, and perished. Then the gods came into their own, and the demons were overcome. He who knows thus comes into his own, and the rival who hates him is overcome. ॥1.3.7॥
1.3.8: They said: Where was he who has thus joined us (to our godhood)? He is within the mouth (ayam āsye antaḥ). So he is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga). ॥1.3.8॥
1.3.9: That deity is named Dūr, for death is far (dūram) from it. Death is far from him who knows thus. ॥1.3.9॥
1.3.10: That deity took away from these deities the evil that is death, and led it to where the end of these quarters is; there it laid down their evils. Therefore one should not go to the people there, nor to that end, thinking: Let me not fall in with evil, with death. ॥1.3.10॥
1.3.11: That deity, having taken away from these deities the evil that is death, then carried them beyond death. ॥1.3.11॥
1.3.12: It carried speech beyond death first. When speech was freed from death, it became fire. This fire, having passed beyond death, blazes beyond it. ॥1.3.12॥
1.3.13: Then it carried prāṇa (the breath of smell) beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the air. This air, having passed beyond death, blows beyond it. ॥1.3.13॥
1.3.14: Then it carried the eye beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the sun. That sun, having passed beyond death, shines beyond it. ॥1.3.14॥
1.3.15: Then it carried the ear beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the quarters. These quarters have passed beyond death and are beyond it. ॥1.3.15॥
1.3.16: Then it carried the mind beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the moon. That moon, having passed beyond death, shines beyond it. So indeed this deity carries beyond death him who knows thus. ॥1.3.16॥
1.3.17: Then it won for itself, by its chanting, the food to be eaten; for whatever food is eaten is eaten by this (prāṇa) alone, and in that food it stands firm here. ॥1.3.17॥
1.3.18: The gods said: All this is just this much, the food; and you have won it for yourself by chanting. Now give us too a share in this food. Prāṇa said: Then enter into me from all sides. The gods said: So be it. They entered into it and settled all around it. Therefore whatever food one eats by it, by that these (speech and the rest) are satisfied. So indeed do his own people gather round him who knows thus: he becomes the support of his own, their best and their leader, an eater of food (free of sickness) and their master. But whoever among his own people wishes to be a rival to one who knows thus is not able to support his dependents; while he who follows him, or who, following him, wishes to support his dependents, he alone is able to support his dependents. ॥1.3.18॥
1.3.19: He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga). Prāṇa indeed is the essence of the limbs. Prāṇa, as all know, is the essence of the limbs; therefore from whatever limb prāṇa departs, that very limb dries up there, for it is the essence of the limbs. ॥1.3.19॥
1.3.20: He is Bṛhaspati too. Speech is bṛhatī (the Ṛk), and he is its lord (pati); therefore he is Bṛhaspati. ॥1.3.20॥
1.3.21: He is Brahmaṇaspati too. Speech is brahman (the Yajus), and he is its lord; therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati. ॥1.3.21॥
1.3.22: He is the sāman, the chant, too. Speech is sā, and this (prāṇa) is ama: sā and ama, that is why the sāman is called sāman. Or else, because he is the same as a tiny insect (pluṣi), the same as a mosquito, the same as an elephant, the same as these three worlds, the same as this whole (universe), for that reason too he is the sāman. He who knows this sāman thus attains union with the sāman and a place in its world. ॥1.3.22॥
1.3.23: He is the udgītha too. Prāṇa is ut, for by prāṇa all this is held up. Speech alone is gīthā (song); ut and gīthā: so he is the udgītha. ॥1.3.23॥
1.3.24: On this, too, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while drinking the king (Soma), said: May this king make the head of this man (myself) fall off, if Ayāsya Āṅgirasa chanted the udgītha by any other than this (prāṇa). For he chanted it with speech and with prāṇa alone. ॥1.3.24॥
1.3.25: He who knows the wealth (sva) of this sāman comes to have wealth. Its tone (svara) is its wealth. Therefore one who is about to do the priest's work should wish for a (good) tone in his voice, and with that voice rich in tone he should do the priest's work. That is why at a sacrifice people long to see one who has a (good) tone, as they long to see one who has wealth. Wealth comes to him who knows thus the wealth of this sāman. ॥1.3.25॥
1.3.26: He who knows the gold (suvarṇa) of this sāman comes to have gold. Its tone is its gold. Gold comes to him who knows thus the gold of this sāman. ॥1.3.26॥
Suvarṇa means both gold and a fine sound (su-varṇa); Śaṅkara takes the fruit to be gold itself.
1.3.27: He who knows the support (pratiṣṭhā) of this sāman stands firm. Its support is speech alone; for it is resting on speech that this prāṇa is sung so. Some say: on food. ॥1.3.27॥
1.3.28: Now, then, the abhyāroha (the recitation of ascent), for the pavamāna hymns alone. The prastotṛ (the priest who sings the opening) begins the sāman. When he begins it, then (the sacrificer) should repeat these: Lead me from the untrue (asat) to the true (sat). Lead me from darkness (tamas) to light (jyotis). Lead me from death (mṛtyu) to immortality (amṛta). When it says, Lead me from the untrue to the true, death is the untrue and immortality the true: Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal, is what it says. Lead me from darkness to light: death is darkness and immortality is light: Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal, is what it says. Lead me from death to immortality: here nothing is hidden, as it were. Then in the other hymns of praise (the udgātṛ) should win by chanting food to eat for himself. So in them (the sacrificer) should ask as a boon whatever wish he wishes. This udgātṛ who knows thus wins by his chanting whatever wish he wishes, for himself or for the sacrificer. This (knowledge) indeed wins the world. He who knows this sāman thus need never pray against being left without a world. ॥1.3.28॥
1.4.1: In the beginning this was the self (ātman) alone, in the form of a person. Looking around, he saw nothing other than himself. He said first: I am. From that he came to be named I (aham). That is why even now, when a man is called, he first says, It is I, and then tells whatever other name he has. Because, being before (pūrva) all this, he burnt up (auṣat) all evils, he is puruṣa. He who knows thus burns up him who wishes to be before him. ॥1.4.1॥
Śaṅkara takes this self as Prajāpati (Virāṭ), the first embodied being, born as the fruit of Vedic knowledge and rites.
1.4.2: He was afraid; that is why one who is alone is afraid. He reflected: Since there is nothing other than me, of what am I afraid? At that his fear left him. Of what should he have been afraid? It is from a second that fear arises. ॥1.4.2॥
1.4.3: He found no delight; that is why one who is alone finds no delight. He wished for a second. He became as large as a woman and a man in close embrace. He made this very self fall into two. From that came husband (pati) and wife (patnī). Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say, this (body) is one's own half, like one half of a split pea. Therefore this space is filled by the woman. He united with her; from that, human beings were born. ॥1.4.3॥
Śaṅkara names the two Manu and Śatarūpā, his daughter.
1.4.4: She reflected: How can he unite with me, having brought me forth from himself? Well, let me hide. She became a cow, the other a bull; he united with her, and from that cattle were born. She became a mare, the other a stallion; she became a she-ass, the other a he-ass; he united with her, and from that the one-hoofed animals were born. She became a she-goat, the other a he-goat; she became a ewe, the other a ram; he united with her, and from that goats and sheep were born. In this way he created all that exists in pairs, down to the ants. ॥1.4.4॥
1.4.5: He knew: I myself am this creation, for it is I who created all this. From that he came to be called creation (sṛṣṭi). He who knows thus comes to be (a creator) in this creation of his. ॥1.4.5॥
1.4.6: Then he churned thus (his hands at his mouth), and from the mouth, as from a womb, and from the hands he created fire. Therefore both of these are hairless on the inside, for the womb is hairless on the inside. As for what they say of each god in turn, Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one: that is his manifold creation, for he himself is all the gods. And whatever is moist here he created from his seed; that is Soma. All this is just so much: food and its eater. Soma is food; fire is its eater. This is the higher creation (atisṛṣṭi) of Brahmā: that he created the gods, who are better than he, and that, though mortal, he created immortals. Therefore it is the higher creation. He who knows thus comes to be (a creator) in this higher creation of his. ॥1.4.6॥
1.4.7: At that time this (world) was unmanifest. It became manifest by name and form alone: this one has such a name, this one such a form. Even now it becomes manifest by name and form alone: this one has such a name, this one such a form. He (the Self) has entered here, up to the tips of the nails, as a razor might be laid in a razor-case, or fire (viśvambhara, the all-sustaining) in its nest (the wood). They do not see him, for (so) he is incomplete. Breathing, he is named prāṇa, the vital breath; speaking, speech; seeing, the eye; hearing, the ear; thinking, the mind: these are only the names of his acts. Whoever worships these one by one does not know, for with each of them alone he is incomplete. One should worship him as the Self alone, for in him all these become one. Of all this, this Self is what is to be traced, for by it one knows all this. As one finds (a lost animal) by its footprints, so he who knows thus finds fame and the company of those dear to him. ॥1.4.7॥
Śloka usually means praise or renown; Śaṅkara takes it here as union with those dear to one.
1.4.8: Dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than anything else, for it is innermost: that is this Self. If one speaks of something other than the Self as dear, (he who holds the Self dear) may say to him: What you hold dear will be cut off (will perish); he has the power to say so, and so indeed it would be. One should worship the Self alone as dear. Whoever worships only the Self as dear: what he holds dear does not perish. ॥1.4.8॥
1.4.9: (Those who seek Brahman) say: Men think that by the knowledge of Brahman, the supreme Self, they will become all. What, then, did that Brahman know, by which it became all? ॥1.4.9॥
1.4.10: In the beginning this was Brahman alone. It knew only itself: I am Brahman. Therefore it became all. Whoever among the gods awoke to it became that; so too among the seers, so too among men. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realised: I became Manu, and the sun. And so now too, whoever knows thus, I am Brahman, becomes all this; even the gods cannot prevent his becoming so, for he becomes their Self. But whoever worships another deity, thinking, He is one being and I am another, does not know. As a domestic animal (is to men), so is he to the gods. Just as many animals serve a man, so each man serves the gods. Even when one animal is taken away it is unpleasant; how much more when many are. Therefore it does not please them that men should know this. ॥1.4.10॥

Śaṅkara takes Brahman here as the Self that has entered the bodies (1.4.7), Brahman even before it knew itself; he sets aside the readings that it is the lower Brahman (Prajāpati) or a man still to become Brahman.
1.4.11: In the beginning this was the brahman (the priestly order) alone, one only. Being one, it did not flourish. It created a better form, the kṣatra (the ruling order): those who are rulers among the gods, Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, Īśāna. Therefore there is nothing higher than the kṣatra; therefore at the rājasūya (the royal consecration) the brāhmaṇa sits below the kṣatriya and honours him. On the kṣatra alone he bestows that glory of his. The brahman is the source (yoni) of the kṣatra. So, though the king attains supremacy, at the end he rests on the brahman, his own source. Whoever harms him (the brāhmaṇa) strikes at his own source. He becomes the more sinful, like one who harms a better man. ॥1.4.11॥
Here brahman is the priestly order; Śaṅkara takes it as Prajāpati, who had become fire and identified himself with the brāhmaṇa caste.
1.4.12: Still he did not flourish. He created the viś (the order of the people): those kinds of gods who are named in groups, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts. ॥1.4.12॥
1.4.13: Still he did not flourish. He created the śūdra order, Pūṣan. This (earth) is Pūṣan, for she nourishes all this, whatever there is. ॥1.4.13॥
1.4.14: Still he did not flourish. He created a better form, dharma, the law of right. This dharma is the ruler of the ruler (the kṣatra of the kṣatra); therefore there is nothing higher than dharma. So even a weaker man hopes to prevail over a stronger one through dharma, as one does through a king. That which is dharma is truth. Therefore of one who speaks the truth they say, He speaks dharma, and of one who speaks dharma, He speaks the truth; for both of these are this alone (dharma). ॥1.4.14॥
1.4.15: So these are the brahman, the kṣatra, the viś and the śūdra. Among the gods the brahman became (the brahman) as fire alone, among men as the brāhmaṇa; it became the kṣatriya through the kṣatriya, the vaiśya through the vaiśya, the śūdra through the śūdra. Therefore people seek a world (the fruit of their rites) among the gods in fire alone, and among men in the brāhmaṇa; for in these two forms the brahman came to be. Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world (the Self), that world, being unknown, does not protect him, any more than the Veda not recited, or any other work not done. Even if one who does not know thus does a great holy work, it is surely exhausted for him in the end. One should worship the Self alone as one's world. He who worships the Self alone as his world, his work is not exhausted, for out of this very Self he creates whatever he desires. ॥1.4.15॥
1.4.16: Now this self (the householder) is a world for all beings. In that he offers oblations and sacrifices, he is the world of the gods; in that he recites (the Veda), of the seers; in that he makes offerings to the ancestors and desires offspring, of the ancestors; in that he gives men shelter and gives them food, of men; in that he finds grass and water for animals, of animals; in that beasts and birds, down to the ants, live (on what is) in his houses, he is their world. As one would wish safety for one's own world (one's body), so all beings always wish safety for him who knows thus. This has been known and has been examined. ॥1.4.16॥
1.4.17: In the beginning this was the self alone, one only. He desired: May I have a wife; then may I be born (as offspring); then may I have wealth; then may I do work. Such indeed is the whole of desire; even wishing, one would not find more than this. That is why even now one who is alone desires: May I have a wife; then may I be born (as offspring); then may I have wealth; then may I do work. As long as he lacks any one of these, so long he thinks himself incomplete. His completeness is this: The mind is his self, speech his wife, prāṇa his offspring, the eye his human wealth, for with the eye one finds it; the ear his divine wealth, for with the ear one hears it; the body (ātman) is his work, for with the body one does work. This sacrifice is fivefold (pāṅkta); the animal is fivefold; man is fivefold; all this, whatever there is, is fivefold. He who knows thus attains all this. ॥1.4.17॥
Śaṅkara takes this self as the unenlightened man, alone before he takes a wife.
1.5.1: Of the seven foods that the father brought forth by intellect and austerity, one is common to all this; two he gave the gods as their share; for himself he made three; one he gave to the animals. Upon it everything rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not. Why do they not waste away, though they are eaten always? He who knows that imperishableness eats food with his mouth (pratīka); he goes to the gods; he lives on vigour (ūrj). These are the verses. ॥1.5.1॥
Śaṅkara takes intellect and austerity here as knowledge and rites, and the father as the man who by them brings forth the whole world as his food; that world, in its seven parts, is the seven foods.
1.5.2: The father brought forth the seven foods by intellect and austerity: for it was by intellect and austerity that the father brought them forth. One of them is common: this which is eaten is that common food of it. He who worships this is not freed from evil, for it is mixed (shared by all). Two he gave the gods as their share: what is offered into the fire (huta) and what is offered after it (prahuta). That is why people offer into the fire for the gods and make the after-offering too. Some say also that they are the new-moon and the full-moon sacrifices. Therefore one should not be given to offering iṣṭis (sacrifices for things desired). One he gave to the animals: that is milk. For at first men and animals alike live on milk alone. That is why, when a child is born, they first make it lick ghee or give it the breast to suck; and of a calf just born they say: it does not yet eat grass. Upon it everything rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not: for it is on milk that all this rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not. As for what they say, that one who offers milk for a year conquers recurring death (punarmṛtyu), one should not think so. On the very day he offers it, he who knows thus conquers recurring death, for he gives the gods all the food there is to eat. Why do they not waste away, though they are eaten always: the person (puruṣa) indeed is that imperishableness, for he brings forth this food again and again. He who knows that imperishableness: the person indeed is that imperishableness. For he brings forth this food by thought upon thought and by his works; if he did not do so, it would waste away. He eats food with his mouth (pratīka): pratīka is the mouth, so this means with the mouth. He goes to the gods, he lives on vigour: this is praise. ॥1.5.2॥

Śaṅkara takes worship here as living wholly for this food, and mixed as belonging to all, so that not a mouthful can be taken without hurting another. He takes the mouth as being chief: one who knows thus remains the eater of food and does not himself become food.
1.5.3: Three he made for himself: mind, speech and prāṇa, the vital breath; these he made for himself. (People say:) I was with my mind elsewhere, I did not see; I was with my mind elsewhere, I did not hear. For it is with the mind that one sees, with the mind that one hears. Desire, conception (saṅkalpa), doubt, faith, want of faith, steadiness, unsteadiness, shame, understanding, fear: all this is mind alone. That is why, even when touched from behind, one knows it with the mind. Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone; for it follows an end, the thing meant, but it is not itself (a thing made known). Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna and ana: all this is prāṇa alone. This self (the body) is made of these: made of speech, made of mind, made of prāṇa. ॥1.5.3॥
Śaṅkara takes it that speech, like a lamp, makes known the thing meant, but is not itself made known by anything else.
1.5.4: These are the three worlds: speech is this world, mind the mid-region, prāṇa that world yonder. ॥1.5.4॥
1.5.5: These are the three Vedas: speech is the Ṛgveda, mind the Yajurveda, prāṇa the Sāmaveda. ॥1.5.5॥
1.5.6: These are the gods, the ancestors and men: speech is the gods, mind the ancestors, prāṇa men. ॥1.5.6॥
1.5.7: These are father, mother and offspring: mind is the father, speech the mother, prāṇa the offspring. ॥1.5.7॥
1.5.8: These are the known, what is sought to be known, and the unknown. Whatever is known is a form of speech, for speech is the known; speech, becoming that, protects him (who knows thus). ॥1.5.8॥
1.5.9: Whatever is sought to be known is a form of mind, for mind is what is sought to be known; mind, becoming that, protects him. ॥1.5.9॥
1.5.10: Whatever is unknown is a form of prāṇa, for prāṇa is the unknown; prāṇa, becoming that, protects him. ॥1.5.10॥
1.5.11: Of that speech the earth is the body, and this fire its luminous form. However far speech reaches, so far reaches the earth, and so far this fire. ॥1.5.11॥
1.5.12: And of this mind heaven is the body, and yonder sun its luminous form. However far mind reaches, so far reaches heaven, and so far yonder sun. The two came together in union; from that prāṇa was born. He is Indra; he is without a rival. A second, indeed, is a rival. He who knows thus has no rival. ॥1.5.12॥
1.5.13: And of this prāṇa water is the body, and yonder moon its luminous form. However far prāṇa reaches, so far reaches water, and so far yonder moon. These are all alike, all infinite. He who worships them as finite wins a finite world; and he who worships them as infinite wins an infinite world. ॥1.5.13॥
1.5.14: This Prajāpati is the year, with sixteen parts (kalā). His nights (the lunar days) are fifteen parts; his sixteenth part is constant. By the nights alone he waxes and wanes. On the new-moon night he enters, by this sixteenth part, into all that has breath here, and then is born the next morning. Therefore on that night one should not cut off the prāṇa of any living creature, not even of a lizard, in honour of that very deity. ॥1.5.14॥
Śaṅkara takes Prajāpati here as the moon, waxing and waning by the lunar days; on the new-moon night it dwells in living beings as the water they drink and the plants they eat.
1.5.15: That Prajāpati who is the year, with sixteen parts, is this very person who knows thus. His wealth is the fifteen parts; his self (the body) is his sixteenth part. By wealth alone he waxes and wanes. This self (the body) is the hub, and wealth the rim. Therefore, even if he is stripped of everything, if he lives on in his self, people only say: he has lost his rim. ॥1.5.15॥
1.5.16: Now there are three worlds indeed: the world of men, the world of the ancestors, the world of the gods. This world of men can be won by a son alone, by no other work; the world of the ancestors by rites, the world of the gods by knowledge. The world of the gods is the best of worlds; therefore they praise knowledge. ॥1.5.16॥
1.5.17: Now, then, the handing over (sampratti). When (a father) thinks he is about to depart, he says to his son: You are brahman (the Veda), you are the sacrifice, you are the world. In reply the son says: I am brahman, I the sacrifice, I the world. Of whatever has been studied, the oneness of all of it is in (the word) brahman. Whatever sacrifices there are, the oneness of all of them is in (the word) sacrifice. Whatever worlds there are, the oneness of all of them is in (the word) world. All this is indeed just this much. (He thinks:) This (son), being all this, will protect me from this (world). That is why they call a son who has been taught lokya (one who wins the world for his father); that is why they teach him. When one who knows thus departs from this world, he enters into his son together with these very prāṇas (speech, mind and prāṇa). If anything has been left undone by him through some lapse, the son frees him from all of it. That is why he is called a son (putra). Through his son alone he stands firm in this world; then these divine, immortal prāṇas enter him. ॥1.5.17॥
Śaṅkara explains the name putra: by filling what the father left undone, the son saves (trā) him.
1.5.18: Out of the earth and out of fire, divine speech enters him. That is divine speech, by which whatever he says comes to be. ॥1.5.18॥
1.5.19: Out of heaven and out of the sun, divine mind enters him. That is divine mind, by which he is ever joyful and does not grieve. ॥1.5.19॥
1.5.20: Out of water and out of the moon, divine prāṇa enters him. That is divine prāṇa which, whether moving or not moving, is neither troubled nor harmed. He who knows thus becomes the Self of all beings. As this deity is, so is he. As all beings protect and honour this deity, so all beings protect and honour him who knows thus. Whatever sorrow these creatures feel stays with them; only good (puṇya) goes to him. Evil does not go to the gods. ॥1.5.20॥
1.5.21: Now, then, an inquiry into the vow (vrata). Prajāpati created the organs (karmāṇi, the instruments of acts). Once created, they vied with one another. Speech took the vow: I will keep on speaking. The eye: I will keep on seeing. The ear: I will keep on hearing. So did the other organs, each by its own act. Death, becoming weariness, seized them; he reached them, and having reached them, Death held them back. That is why speech tires, the eye tires, the ear tires. But this one he did not reach, this prāṇa in the middle. They resolved to know it: This indeed is the best of us, which, whether moving or not moving, is neither troubled nor harmed. Come, let us all become a form of this one. They all became a form of this one. That is why they are called by its name, prāṇas. By the name of him who knows thus, people call the family into which he is born. And whoever vies with one who knows thus dries up, and having dried up, dies at last. So much as regards the body (adhyātma). ॥1.5.21॥
1.5.22: Now as regards the gods (adhidaivata). Fire took the vow: I will keep on burning. The sun: I will keep on giving heat. The moon: I will keep on shining. So did the other deities, each according to its divine nature. As the prāṇa in the middle is among these prāṇas, so is Vāyu, the wind, among these deities; for the other deities set, but not Vāyu. Vāyu is the deity that never sets. ॥1.5.22॥
1.5.23: Now on this there is a verse: That from which the sun rises and that in which it sets — it rises from prāṇa and sets in prāṇa — that the gods made their law (dharma); it alone is today, and it tomorrow. For what they held to then, that they do even today. Therefore one should keep one vow alone: one should go on breathing with prāṇa and with apāna, thinking: Let evil, death, not reach me. And if he keeps it, he should wish to carry it through. By it he attains union with this deity and a place in its world. ॥1.5.23॥
1.6.1: This (world) is indeed a triad: name, form and action. Of these, of names, speech is their uktha (source), for from it all names arise (ut-thā). It is their sāman, for it is equal (sama) to all names; it is their brahman, for it upholds all names. ॥1.6.1॥
1.6.2: Now of forms, the eye is their uktha, for from it all forms arise. It is their sāman, for it is equal to all forms. It is their brahman, for it upholds all forms. ॥1.6.2॥
1.6.3: Now of actions, the self (the body) is their uktha, for from it all actions arise; it is their sāman, for it is equal to all actions; it is their brahman, for it upholds all actions. These three, while three, are one: this self; and the self, while one, is these three. This is the immortal, veiled by the true (satya). Prāṇa, the vital breath, indeed is the immortal; name and form are the true; by these two this prāṇa is veiled. ॥1.6.3॥
Śaṅkara takes the true (satya) here as the visible, mortal body made of name and form, and the immortal as the prāṇa within that holds it up.
2.1.1: Om. There was once Dṛpta-Bālāki (the proud Bālāki) of Garga's line (Gārgya), learned in the Veda and skilled in speech. He said to Ajātaśatru, king of Kāśī: Let me tell you of Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: For this word alone we give a thousand (cows). People run (to Janaka), saying: Janaka, Janaka. ॥2.1.1॥
Śaṅkara: people run to Janaka as to one who gives and one who listens; the king means that Gārgya has thought the same of him.
2.1.2: Gārgya said: The person who is in the sun yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the one who stands above all, the head of all beings, the king. He who worships him thus stands above all, and becomes the head of all beings, a king. ॥2.1.2॥

Śaṅkara: Gārgya knows Brahman only as an object of ignorance; each person he names is a deity present outside (here in the sun) and in the body (here in the eye), seated in the heart as doer and enjoyer; Ajātaśatru's No, no means: this I know already.
2.1.3: Gārgya said: The person who is in the moon yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the great one, white-robed, Soma the king. He who worships him thus has Soma pressed for him day after day, and pressed in plenty, and his food does not fail. ॥2.1.3॥
2.1.4: Gārgya said: The person who is in the lightning yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the radiant one. He who worships him thus becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant. ॥2.1.4॥
2.1.5: Gārgya said: This person who is in space, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the full and the unmoving. He who worships him thus is filled with offspring and cattle, and his offspring do not die out from this world. ॥2.1.5॥
2.1.6: Gārgya said: This person who is in the air, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as Indra, Vaikuṇṭha (the irresistible), the unconquered army. He who worships him thus becomes victorious, never conquered, a conqueror of those who stand against him. ॥2.1.6॥
2.1.7: Gārgya said: This person who is in fire, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the all-withstanding (viṣāsahi). He who worships him thus becomes all-withstanding, and his offspring become all-withstanding. ॥2.1.7॥
2.1.8: Gārgya said: This person who is in the waters, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the fitting one (pratirūpa). He who worships him thus has what is fitting come to him, not what is unfitting, and from him is born one who is fitting. ॥2.1.8॥
Śaṅkara takes pratirūpa as fitting, in keeping with śruti and smṛti; the word can also mean a likeness or image.
2.1.9: Gārgya said: This person who is in the mirror, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the shining one. He who worships him thus becomes shining, and his offspring become shining; and he outshines all those he comes together with. ॥2.1.9॥
2.1.10: Gārgya said: This sound that rises after a man as he walks, this alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make it a matter of talk (with me). I worship it as life (asu). He who worships it thus reaches his full span of life in this world; prāṇa, the vital breath, does not leave him before his time. ॥2.1.10॥
2.1.11: Gārgya said: This person who is in the quarters, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the second who never departs. He who worships him thus comes to have a companion, and his company (of his own people) is not cut off from him. ॥2.1.11॥
2.1.12: Gārgya said: This person made of shadow, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as death. He who worships him thus reaches his full span of life in this world; death does not come to him before his time. ॥2.1.12॥
2.1.13: Gārgya said: This person who is in the self, him alone I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the self-possessed (ātmanvin). He who worships him thus becomes self-possessed, and his offspring become self-possessed. Gārgya fell silent. ॥2.1.13॥
2.1.14: Ajātaśatru said: Is this all? Gārgya said: This is all. Ajātaśatru said: By this much (Brahman) is not known. Gārgya said: Let me come to you (as a pupil). ॥2.1.14॥
2.1.15: Ajātaśatru said: It goes against the natural order that a brāhmaṇa should come to a kṣatriya, thinking: He will tell me of Brahman. Still, I shall make you know it clearly. He took him by the hand and rose. The two came to a man who was asleep. He called to him by these names: O great one, white-robed one, Soma, king! He did not get up. He woke him by pressing him again and again with his hand. He got up. ॥2.1.15॥
Śaṅkara: the sleeper does not answer to the names of the prāṇa Gārgya worshipped, yet wakes when pressed: so the experiencer is other than prāṇa.
2.1.16: Ajātaśatru said: When he was asleep thus, where was this person made of understanding (vijñānamaya) then, and from where has he come back? Gārgya did not know this. ॥2.1.16॥
2.1.17: Ajātaśatru said: When he was asleep thus, this person made of understanding, taking by his understanding the understanding of these prāṇas (the organs), lies in the space that is within the heart. When he takes them in, then the man is named: he sleeps (svapiti). Then prāṇa (the sense of smell) is held in, speech is held in, the eye is held in, the ear is held in, the mind is held in. ॥2.1.17॥
Śaṅkara takes the space within the heart as the supreme Self, and svapiti as svam apīti, he has gone into his own (Self).
2.1.18: When he moves about in dream, those are his worlds: then he becomes a great king, as it were, or a great brāhmaṇa, as it were, or goes, as it were, to states high and low. As a great king, taking the people of his land with him, would move about as he pleases in his own country, so this one, taking the prāṇas (the organs) with him, moves about as he pleases in his own body. ॥2.1.18॥
2.1.19: Now, when he is in deep sleep, when he knows nothing whatever: there are seventy-two thousand channels called hitā, which spread out from the heart into the purītat (the membrane around the heart); gliding back through them, he lies in the purītat. As a young child, or a great king, or a great brāhmaṇa might lie at rest, having reached the height of bliss that wipes out all sorrow, so does this one lie. ॥2.1.19॥
Śaṅkara takes the purītat here as standing for the whole body, which the self pervades as fire pervades a heated ball of iron.
2.1.20: As a spider moves up along its thread, and as tiny sparks fly out from a fire, so from this Self come forth all the prāṇas (the organs), all the worlds, all the gods, all beings. Its secret name (upaniṣad) is: the truth of the truth. The prāṇas are truth, and this is their truth. ॥2.1.20॥
Śaṅkara: upaniṣad here is the name that brings the Self near; the next two brāhmaṇas explain it, and the Self from which all come forth is the supreme Self.
2.2.1: He who knows the young one (śiśu) with its seat (ādhāna), its further seat (pratyādhāna), its post and its tether, holds back seven rivals who hate him. This young one is truly the middle prāṇa, the vital breath; this (body) is its seat, this (head) its further seat, prāṇa (strength) its post, food its tether. ॥2.2.1॥

Śaṅkara: the young one is the subtle body in the middle of the body, like a calf; the seven rivals are the seven openings of the head and the attachments they breed, which turn the sight outward, away from the Self.
2.2.2: These seven imperishable ones (akṣiti) attend on it: through the red streaks in the eye Rudra is bound to it; through the water in the eye, Parjanya; through the pupil, Āditya (the sun); through the black (of the eye), Agni; through the white, Indra; through the lower eyelid the earth is bound to it, through the upper, heaven. The food of him who knows thus does not fail. ॥2.2.2॥
2.2.3: On this there is a verse: There is a bowl with its mouth below and its bottom above; in it is set glory of every form. On its rim sit seven seers; speech is the eighth, in converse with brahman. A bowl with its mouth below and its bottom above: this is the head, for it is a bowl with its mouth below and its bottom above. In it is set glory of every form: the prāṇas are truly glory of every form; it is the prāṇas that this means. On its rim sit seven seers: the prāṇas are truly the seers; it is the prāṇas that this means. Speech is the eighth, in converse with brahman: for speech is the eighth, and it converses with brahman. ॥2.2.3॥
2.2.4: These two (ears) are Gotama and Bharadvāja: this one is Gotama, this one Bharadvāja. These two (eyes) are Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni: this one is Viśvāmitra, this one Jamadagni. These two (nostrils) are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa: this one is Vasiṣṭha, this one Kaśyapa. Speech is Atri, for by speech food is eaten; the name Atri is truly atti, the eater. He who knows thus becomes the eater of all, and all becomes his food. ॥2.2.4॥
Śaṅkara: in each pair the right is named first, or the reverse; and speech, as Atri the eater, is the seventh seer.
2.3.1: Brahman has just two forms: the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal, the fixed and the moving (yat), the definite (sat) and the beyond (tyat). ॥2.3.1॥

Śaṅkara: these are the forms, superimposed by ignorance, through which the formless Brahman is described; sat is what can be marked off from others, tyat what can only be spoken of indirectly, as that.
2.3.2: The formed is whatever is other than air and the mid-region: this is mortal, this is fixed, this is the definite (sat). Of this formed, this mortal, this fixed, this definite, the essence is he who shines (the sun), since this is the essence of the definite. ॥2.3.2॥
2.3.3: Now the formless: air and the mid-region. This is immortal, this is the moving, this is the beyond. Of this formless, this immortal, this moving, this beyond, the essence is the person in this orb (of the sun), since this is the essence of the beyond. So much with regard to the gods. ॥2.3.3॥
Śaṅkara takes this person as Hiraṇyagarbha, who is called prāṇa.
2.3.4: Now with regard to the self (the body): the formed is just this, whatever is other than prāṇa, the vital breath, and this space within the body; this is mortal, this is fixed, this is the definite. Of this formed, this mortal, this fixed, this definite, the essence is the eye, since this is the essence of the definite. ॥2.3.4॥
2.3.5: Now the formless: prāṇa and this space within the body. This is immortal, this is the moving, this is the beyond. Of this formless, this immortal, this moving, this beyond, the essence is this person in the right eye, since this is the essence of the beyond. ॥2.3.5॥
2.3.6: The form of this person is this: like a cloth dyed with turmeric, like pale white wool, like the indragopa (the red cochineal insect), like a flame of fire, like a white lotus, like a single flash of lightning. Like a single flash of lightning is the glory of him who knows thus. Now, therefore, the teaching: not thus, not thus (neti neti); for there is no other, higher (teaching) than this: not thus. Then the name: the truth of the truth. The prāṇas are truth, and this is their truth. ॥2.3.6॥

Śaṅkara takes these forms as the impressions (vāsanā) of the subtle person, coloured as a dyed cloth is; not thus, not thus points to Brahman by denying every attribute, and there is no other, higher description of it than this.
2.4.1: Yājñavalkya said: Maitreyī, my dear, I am about to rise up from this station (the householder's life). Come, let me make a settlement between you and Kātyāyanī here (dividing what I have). ॥2.4.1॥
2.4.2: Maitreyī said: Revered sir, if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, how would I become immortal by it? Yājñavalkya said: No. Your life would be just like the life of those who have plenty of means; but through wealth there is no hope of immortality. ॥2.4.2॥
2.4.3: Maitreyī said: What should I do with that which would not make me immortal? Tell me just what you, revered sir, know (of the way to immortality). ॥2.4.3॥
2.4.4: Yājñavalkya said: Ah, my dear, you have been dear to us, and now you speak what is dear. Come, sit down; I shall explain it to you. But while I explain, meditate deeply on what I say. ॥2.4.4॥
2.4.5: Yājñavalkya said: Not for the sake of the husband, my dear, is the husband dear; the husband is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the wife, my dear, is the wife dear; the wife is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of sons, my dear, are sons dear; sons are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of wealth, my dear, is wealth dear; wealth is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the priestly class (brahman), my dear, is the priestly class dear; the priestly class is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the ruling class (kṣatra), my dear, is the ruling class dear; the ruling class is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the worlds, my dear, are the worlds dear; the worlds are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the gods, my dear, are the gods dear; the gods are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of beings, my dear, are beings dear; beings are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of all, my dear, is all dear; all is dear for the sake of the Self. It is the Self, my dear, that is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected on, to be meditated on. Maitreyī, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, reflected on and known, all this is known. ॥2.4.5॥
Śaṅkara: the Self is first heard of from the teacher and the scripture, then reflected on by reasoning, then meditated on with certainty; so it comes to be seen.
2.4.6: The priestly class rejects him who knows the priestly class as other than the Self; the ruling class rejects him who knows the ruling class as other than the Self; the worlds reject him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods reject him who knows the gods as other than the Self; beings reject him who knows beings as other than the Self; all rejects him who knows all as other than the Self. This priestly class, this ruling class, these worlds, these gods, these beings, all this, is what this Self is. ॥2.4.6॥
2.4.7: It is as with a drum being beaten: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. ॥2.4.7॥
2.4.8: It is as with a conch being blown: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the conch, or the one who blows the conch, the sound is grasped. ॥2.4.8॥
2.4.9: It is as with a vīṇā being played: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the vīṇā, or the one who plays the vīṇā, the sound is grasped. ॥2.4.9॥
2.4.10: As from a fire laid with damp fuel clouds of smoke go forth in many ways, so, my dear, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa (the Atharvaveda), the itihāsa (histories), the purāṇa (ancient lore), the vidyās (sciences), the Upaniṣads, the ślokas (verses), the sūtras (aphorisms), the anuvyākhyānas (explanations) and the vyākhyānas (commentaries) are the breathing out of this great Being; all these are breathed out by this one alone. ॥2.4.10॥
Śaṅkara: the itihāsa, purāṇa, vidyās and the rest here are parts of the Veda's own brāhmaṇa portion (such as the dialogue of Urvaśī and Purūravas), not separate books.
2.4.11: As the ocean is the one place where all waters meet (ekāyana), so the skin is the one meeting place of all touches, the nose of all smells, the tongue of all tastes, the eye of all forms, the ear of all sounds, the mind of all resolves, the heart of all knowledge, the two hands of all actions, the organ of generation of all joys, the anus of all excretions, the two feet of all journeys, and speech of all the Vedas. ॥2.4.11॥
2.4.12: As a lump of salt dropped into water dissolves into the water itself, and none can take it out again, but from wherever one takes (the water), it is salt, so, my dear, this great Being, endless and boundless, is a mass of consciousness alone. Arising out of these elements, it vanishes along with them; after departing (from the body) there is no consciousness (saṃjñā). This is what I say, my dear: so said Yājñavalkya. ॥2.4.12॥

Śaṅkara: what arises out of the elements and vanishes with them is the self's separateness, made by ignorance through the body and organs; and what is not there after departing is particular consciousness (I am so-and-so, this is mine), not consciousness itself, which is the mass of consciousness.
2.4.13: Maitreyī said: Just here, revered sir, you have bewildered me, (by saying that) after departing there is no consciousness. Yājñavalkya said: I am not saying anything bewildering, my dear; this (as I have told it), my dear, is enough for understanding. ॥2.4.13॥
2.4.14: For where there is duality, as it were, there one smells another, one sees another, one hears another, one speaks to another, one thinks of another, one knows another. But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then with what should one smell whom, with what should one see whom, with what should one hear whom, with what should one speak to whom, with what should one think of whom, with what should one know whom? By what should one know that by which one knows all this? By what, my dear, should one know the knower? ॥2.4.14॥
2.5.1: This earth is the honey of all beings; of this earth, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this earth, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the bodily one (śārīra): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.1॥
Śaṅkara: honey here means effect: as one honeycomb is made by many bees, so the earth is made by all beings, and all beings are its effect; each serves the other, and so all come from one cause.
2.5.2: These waters are the honey of all beings; of these waters, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in these waters, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in the seed (raitasa): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.2॥
2.5.3: This fire is the honey of all beings; of this fire, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this fire, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is made of speech: he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.3॥
2.5.4: This air is the honey of all beings; of this air, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this air, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is prāṇa, the vital breath: he is just this Self. This is the immortal. This is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.4॥
2.5.5: This sun is the honey of all beings; of this sun, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this sun, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in the eye (cākṣuṣa): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.5॥
2.5.6: These quarters are the honey of all beings; of these quarters, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in these quarters, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in the ear (śrautra), present at the time of hearing (prātiśrutka): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.6॥
2.5.7: This moon is the honey of all beings; of this moon, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this moon, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in the mind (mānasa): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.7॥
2.5.8: This lightning is the honey of all beings; of this lightning, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this lightning, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in the radiance of the skin (taijasa): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.8॥
2.5.9: This thunder is the honey of all beings; of this thunder, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this thunder, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in sound (śābda), in the voice (sauvara): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.9॥
2.5.10: This space is the honey of all beings; of this space, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this space, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the space in the heart: he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.10॥
2.5.11: This dharma (the law of right conduct) is the honey of all beings; of this dharma, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this dharma, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in dharma (dhārma): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.11॥
2.5.12: This truth is the honey of all beings; of this truth, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this truth, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the one in truth (sātya): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.12॥
2.5.13: This humankind is the honey of all beings; of this humankind, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this humankind, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who within the body is the human one (mānuṣa): he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.13॥
2.5.14: This self is the honey of all beings; of this self, all beings are the honey. The person made of light, made of immortality, who is in this self, and the person made of light, made of immortality, who is this self: he is just this Self. This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. ॥2.5.14॥

Śaṅkara: "this self" here is the body and organs taken as a whole, joined with all beings and gods; and the person who is this self is the self made of understanding (vijñānamaya), for whose sake that whole exists.
2.5.15: This Self is indeed the overlord of all beings, the king of all beings. As all the spokes are held fast in the hub and in the rim of a chariot wheel, so in this Self all beings, all gods, all worlds, all prāṇas (the organs), all these selves are held fast. ॥2.5.15॥
Śaṅkara: this Self here is the knower of Brahman, who (by this knowledge) has become the Self of all; the selves are those that have entered each body, like the moon's reflections in water.
2.5.16: This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, taught the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: O men (Aśvins), that fierce deed of yours, done for gain, I make known, as thunder makes known the rain: when Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, taught you the honey through a horse's head. ॥2.5.16॥
2.5.17: This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, taught the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: O Aśvins, you brought a horse's head to Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan. He, keeping his word, taught you the honey of Tvaṣṭṛ, and also, O Dasras (destroyers of foes), the secret (honey). ॥2.5.17॥
Śaṅkara: the honey of Tvaṣṭṛ is the knowledge belonging to the pravargya rite, and the secret honey is the knowledge of the supreme Self, told in this madhu brāhmaṇa.
2.5.18: This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, taught the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: He made bodies (puras) with two feet, he made bodies with four feet. First, having become a bird, he, the Person (puruṣa), entered the bodies. This Person is the one who lies (puriśaya) in all the bodies (pur); there is nothing he does not cover, nothing he does not fill within. ॥2.5.18॥
Śaṅkara: he who made the bodies is the supreme Lord, and the bird is the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra).
2.5.19: This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, taught the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: He took the likeness of every form; that is for making his own form known. Indra goes about in many forms through his māyās (powers of illusion); for yoked to him are horses, hundreds and ten. He is the horses; he is ten, and thousands, many and endless. That Brahman is this: with nothing before it, nothing after it, nothing within it, nothing outside it. This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all. This is the teaching. ॥2.5.19॥

Śaṅkara: Indra here is the supreme Lord, the māyās are the notions (false identifications) made through name and form, and the horses are the senses (which draw to their objects), hundreds and ten because beings are so many.
2.6.1: Now the line of teachers. Pautimāṣya received this teaching from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya, Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Kauśika, Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya, Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kauśika and from Gautama, Gautama ॥2.6.1॥
Śaṅkara: this is the line of teachers of the Madhu-kāṇḍa (the first two adhyāyas of this Upaniṣad), given in praise of the knowledge of Brahman and for study and recital (japa).
2.6.2: from Āgniveśya, Āgniveśya from Śāṇḍilya and from Ānabhimlāta, Ānabhimlāta from Ānabhimlāta, Ānabhimlāta from Ānabhimlāta, Ānabhimlāta from Gautama, Gautama from Saitava and Prācīnayogya, Saitava and Prācīnayogya from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Bhāradvāja and from Gautama, Gautama from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Vaijavāpāyana, Vaijavāpāyana from Kauśikāyani, Kauśikāyani ॥2.6.2॥
2.6.3: from Ghṛtakauśika, Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa, Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya, Jātūkarṇya from Āsurāyaṇa and from Yāska, Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi, Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani, Aupajandhani from Āsuri, Āsuri from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Ātreya, Ātreya from Māṇṭi, Māṇṭi from Gautama, Gautama from Gautama, Gautama from Vātsya, Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya, Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita, Kumārahārita from Gālava, Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya, Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava, Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Panthā Saubhara, Panthā Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra, Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra, Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins, the two Aśvins from Dadhyaṅ Ātharvaṇa, Dadhyaṅ Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva, Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana, Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana, Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi, Ekarṣi from Vipracitti, Vipracitti from Vyaṣṭi, Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru, Sanāru from Sanātana, Sanātana from Sanaga, Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin, Parameṣṭhin from Brahman. Brahman is self-existent. Salutation to Brahman. ॥2.6.3॥
Śaṅkara: Parameṣṭhin is Virāṭ, and the Brahman from whom he received it is Hiraṇyagarbha; beyond him there is no line of teachers; the salutation is to the Brahman that is eternal and self-existent.
3.1.1: Om. Janaka Vaideha, king of Videha, performed a sacrifice with many gifts to the priests. Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and the Pañcālas had gathered there. A desire arose in Janaka Vaideha to know: Which of these brāhmaṇas is the most learned in the Veda? He penned in a thousand cows; to the horns of each of them ten pādas (of gold) were tied. ॥3.1.1॥
Śaṅkara: a pāda is a quarter of a pala of gold; five pādas were tied to each horn.
3.1.2: He said to them: Revered brāhmaṇas, let him who is the best knower of Brahman among you drive these cows away. The brāhmaṇas did not dare. Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil (brahmacārin): Gentle Sāmaśravas, drive these away. He drove them away. The brāhmaṇas grew angry: How can he call himself the best knower of Brahman among us? Now Janaka Vaideha had a hotṛ priest, Aśvala. He asked Yājñavalkya: Yājñavalkya, are you then the best knower of Brahman among us? Yājñavalkya said: We bow to the best knower of Brahman; we only want the cows. On that ground Aśvala, the hotṛ, resolved to question him. ॥3.1.2॥
3.1.3: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, all this is reached by death, all this is overpowered by death; by what means does the sacrificer go free beyond the grasp of death? Yājñavalkya said: By the hotṛ priest, by fire, by speech. Speech is the hotṛ of the sacrifice. This speech is this fire; it is the hotṛ; it is freedom, it is complete freedom. ॥3.1.3॥
Śaṅkara: the sacrifice here is the sacrificer; to see speech and the hotṛ as fire is freedom, and the reaching of the state of fire beyond death that it brings is complete freedom.
3.1.4: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, all this is reached by day and night, all this is overpowered by day and night; by what means does the sacrificer go free beyond the grasp of day and night? Yājñavalkya said: By the adhvaryu priest, by the eye, by the sun. The eye is the adhvaryu of the sacrifice. This eye is yonder sun; it is the adhvaryu; it is freedom, it is complete freedom. ॥3.1.4॥
3.1.5: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, all this is reached by the bright and the dark fortnights, all this is overpowered by the bright and the dark fortnights; by what means does the sacrificer go free beyond the grasp of the bright and the dark fortnights? Yājñavalkya said: By the udgātṛ priest, by Vāyu, the air, by prāṇa, the vital breath. Prāṇa is the udgātṛ of the sacrifice. This prāṇa is Vāyu; it is the udgātṛ; it is freedom, it is complete freedom. ॥3.1.5॥
3.1.6: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, this mid-region is, as it were, without support; by what foothold does the sacrificer climb to the heavenly world? Yājñavalkya said: By the brahman priest, by the mind, by the moon. The mind is the brahman priest of the sacrifice. This mind is yonder moon; it is the brahman priest; it is freedom, it is complete freedom. These are the atimokṣas, the ways of freedom beyond death. Now the sampads, the meditations that gain the fruit of rites through a likeness. ॥3.1.6॥
3.1.7: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, with how many kinds of ṛk verses will this hotṛ perform (his part) in this sacrifice today? Yājñavalkya said: With three. Aśvala asked: Which are those three? Yājñavalkya said: The puronuvākyā (the verse recited before the offering), the yājyā (the verse recited at the offering), and, third, the śasyā (the verse of praise). Aśvala asked: What does he win by them? Yājñavalkya said: Whatever here has life. ॥3.1.7॥
3.1.8: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, how many kinds of oblations will this adhvaryu offer in this sacrifice today? Yājñavalkya said: Three. Aśvala asked: Which are those three? Yājñavalkya said: Those that blaze up when offered, those that roar loudly when offered, and those that sink down and lie (in the ground) when offered. Aśvala asked: What does he win by them? Yājñavalkya said: By those that blaze up when offered he wins the world of the gods, for the world of the gods shines, as it were. By those that roar loudly when offered he wins the world of the ancestors, for the world of the ancestors is, as it were, exceedingly (loud). By those that sink down and lie when offered he wins the world of men, for the world of men is, as it were, below. ॥3.1.8॥

Śaṅkara: the oblations that blaze up are of fuel and ghee, those that make a noise are of flesh and the like, those that sink down are of milk and soma; the likeness with the world of the ancestors is the cry of those whom Yama torments in his city Saṃyaminī.
3.1.9: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, with how many deities does this brahman priest guard the sacrifice from the south today? Yājñavalkya said: With one. Aśvala asked: Which is that one? Yājñavalkya said: The mind alone. The mind is endless, the Viśvedevas (the All-gods) are endless; by it he wins an endless world. ॥3.1.9॥
3.1.10: Aśvala said: Yājñavalkya, how many stotriyā verses will this udgātṛ chant in this sacrifice today? Yājñavalkya said: Three. Aśvala asked: Which are those three? Yājñavalkya said: The puronuvākyā, the yājyā, and, third, the śasyā. Aśvala asked: Which are those that relate to the body? Yājñavalkya said: Prāṇa is the puronuvākyā, apāna (the downward breath) the yājyā, vyāna (the breath that pervades the body) the śasyā. Aśvala asked: What does he win by them? Yājñavalkya said: By the puronuvākyā he wins the world of the earth, by the yājyā the world of the mid-region, by the śasyā the world of heaven. Thereupon Aśvala, the hotṛ, fell silent. ॥3.1.10॥
3.2.1: Then Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga questioned him. Ārtabhāga said: Yājñavalkya, how many grahas (graspers) are there, and how many atigrahas (over-graspers)? Yājñavalkya said: Eight grahas, eight atigrahas. Ārtabhāga asked: Those eight grahas and eight atigrahas, which are they? ॥3.2.1॥
3.2.2: Yājñavalkya said: Prāṇa, the vital breath, is a graha. It is seized by the apāna, its atigraha, for it is with the apāna that one smells odours. ॥3.2.2॥
Śaṅkara: prāṇa here is the organ of smell together with the air, and apāna is odour, for the nose smells the odour that the in-drawn breath (apāna) brings to it.
3.2.3: Speech is a graha. It is seized by name, its atigraha, for it is with speech that one speaks names. ॥3.2.3॥
3.2.4: The tongue is a graha. It is seized by taste, its atigraha, for it is with the tongue that one knows tastes. ॥3.2.4॥
3.2.5: The eye is a graha. It is seized by form, its atigraha, for it is with the eye that one sees forms. ॥3.2.5॥
3.2.6: The ear is a graha. It is seized by sound, its atigraha, for it is with the ear that one hears sounds. ॥3.2.6॥
3.2.7: The mind is a graha. It is seized by desire, its atigraha, for it is with the mind that one desires desires. ॥3.2.7॥
3.2.8: The two hands are a graha. It is seized by work, its atigraha, for it is with the hands that one does work. ॥3.2.8॥
3.2.9: The skin is a graha. It is seized by touch, its atigraha, for it is with the skin that one feels touches. These, then, are the eight grahas and eight atigrahas. ॥3.2.9॥
3.2.10: Ārtabhāga said: Yājñavalkya, all this is the food of death; which, then, is the deity whose food is death? Yājñavalkya said: Fire is death, and it is the food of water. One conquers death that comes again. ॥3.2.10॥
3.2.11: Ārtabhāga said: Yājñavalkya, when this man dies, do the prāṇas go up out of him, or not? Yājñavalkya said: No; they are gathered together right here. He swells, he is blown up; blown up, he lies dead. ॥3.2.11॥
Śaṅkara: this man is the freed knower of Brahman; his prāṇas (the senses and their objects) merge in the supreme Self like waves in the sea, and he goes nowhere.
3.2.12: Ārtabhāga said: Yājñavalkya, when this man dies, what does not leave him? Yājñavalkya said: The name. The name is endless, the Viśvedevas are endless; by it he wins an endless world. ॥3.2.12॥
3.2.13: Ārtabhāga said: Yājñavalkya, when the speech of this dead man goes into fire, his prāṇa into the air, his eye into the sun, his mind into the moon, his ear into the quarters, his body into the earth, his self (ātman) into space, the hairs of his body into the plants, the hairs of his head into the trees, and his blood and semen are laid down in the waters, where then is this man? Yājñavalkya said: Gentle Ārtabhāga, give me your hand; we two alone shall know of this; this is not for the two of us (to settle) in a crowd. The two went out and conferred together. What they spoke of was karma, action, and what they praised was karma: one becomes good by good karma, and bad by bad. Thereupon Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga fell silent. ॥3.2.13॥
Śaṅkara: this is the man without right knowledge; ātman here is the space within the heart; and the question is on what support the man takes up a body again, to which the answer is karma.
3.3.1: Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. Bhujyu said: Yājñavalkya, we wandered among the Madras as students keeping a vow (carakas), and came to the house of Patañcala Kāpya. He had a daughter seized by a gandharva. We asked him (the gandharva): Who are you? He said: Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, we then said to him: Where did the Pārikṣitas (the descendants of Parikṣit) go? Where did the Pārikṣitas go, that is what I ask you, Yājñavalkya: where did the Pārikṣitas go? ॥3.3.1॥
3.3.2: Yājñavalkya said: He surely told you: They went to the place where those who perform the horse sacrifice go. Bhujyu asked: And where do those who perform the horse sacrifice go? Yājñavalkya said: This world is as wide as thirty-two days' journeys of the sun's chariot; the earth, twice as wide, surrounds it on all sides; the ocean, twice as wide, surrounds the earth on all sides. There, in between, is a space as fine as a razor's edge or a fly's wing. Indra, becoming a bird (suparṇa), handed them (the Pārikṣitas) to Vāyu, the air; Vāyu placed them in himself and led them to where those who performed the horse sacrifice were. In just this way, as it were, he (the gandharva) praised Vāyu alone. Therefore Vāyu alone is the individual (vyaṣṭi), Vāyu is the whole (samaṣṭi). He who knows thus conquers death that comes again. Thereupon Bhujyu Lāhyāyani fell silent. ॥3.3.2॥

Śaṅkara: the space is the gap between the two halves of the cosmic egg, through which the performers of the horse sacrifice pass out; Indra is the supreme Lord, the fire built up in the horse sacrifice, who takes the form of a bird with wings and tail.
3.4.1: Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him. Uṣasta said: Yājñavalkya, explain to me the immediate and direct Brahman, the Self that is within all. Yājñavalkya said: This is your Self that is within all. Uṣasta asked: Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? Yājñavalkya said: He who breathes with prāṇa, the vital breath, is your Self that is within all; he who breathes down with the apāna (the downward breath) is your Self that is within all; he who breathes through the body with the vyāna (the breath that pervades the body) is your Self that is within all; he who breathes up with the udāna (the upward breath) is your Self that is within all. This, then, is your Self that is within all. ॥3.4.1॥
3.4.2: Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: Just as someone might say, That is a cow, that is a horse, so has this been pointed out by you. Explain to me that very immediate and direct Brahman, the Self that is within all. Yājñavalkya said: This is your Self that is within all. Uṣasta asked: Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? Yājñavalkya said: You cannot see the seer of seeing, you cannot hear the hearer of hearing, you cannot think the thinker of thinking, you cannot know the knower of knowing. This is your Self that is within all. What is other than this is afflicted. Thereupon Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa fell silent. ॥3.4.2॥

Śaṅkara: Uṣasta means that Yājñavalkya, having promised to show the Self directly, has only pointed to it by its signs, such as breathing, as one who promises to show a cow points to it only by signs such as its moving.
3.5.1: Then Kahola Kauṣītakeya questioned him. Kahola said: Yājñavalkya, explain to me that very immediate and direct Brahman, the Self that is within all. Yājñavalkya said: This is your Self that is within all. Kahola asked: Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? Yājñavalkya said: He who passes beyond hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death. Knowing this very Self, brāhmaṇas rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds, and then go about begging alms. For the desire for sons is itself the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is itself the desire for worlds; both of these are only desires. Therefore a brāhmaṇa, having fully gained learning (pāṇḍitya), should wish to abide in strength (bālya). Having fully gained both strength and learning, he becomes a muni, a man of meditation; having fully gained both what is not silence and silence, he becomes a brāhmaṇa. How does that brāhmaṇa live? However he may live, he is just such. What is other than this is afflicted. Thereupon Kahola Kauṣītakeya fell silent. ॥3.5.1॥

Śaṅkara takes bālya from bala, strength (the strength of knowing the Self), and nirvidya as having known fully; another well-known reading takes bālya as the simplicity of a child and nirvidya as having turned away from it.
3.6.1: Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. Gārgī said: Yājñavalkya, all this is woven, warp and woof, in the waters; then in what are the waters woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the air, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what is the air woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the mid-region, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the mid-region woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the gandharvas, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the gandharvas woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the sun, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the sun woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the moon, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the moon woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the stars, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the stars woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of the gods, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of the gods woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of Indra, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of Indra woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of Prajāpati woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: In the worlds of Brahmā, Gārgī. Gārgī asked: Then in what are the worlds of Brahmā woven, warp and woof? Yājñavalkya said: Gārgī, do not question too far, lest your head fall off. You are questioning too far about a deity about whom one must not question too far. Gārgī, do not question too far. Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī fell silent. ॥3.6.1॥
Śaṅkara: Gārgī is asking by inference about the deity that can be known from scripture alone; that is why her question goes too far.
3.7.1: Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. Uddālaka said: Yājñavalkya, we lived among the Madras in the house of Patañcala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice. His wife was seized by a gandharva. We asked him (the gandharva): Who are you? He said: Kabandha Ātharvaṇa. He said to Patañcala Kāpya and to those who studied the sacrifice: Kāpya, do you know that thread by which this world, the other world and all beings are strung together? Patañcala Kāpya said: I do not know it, revered sir. He said to Patañcala Kāpya and to those who studied the sacrifice: Kāpya, do you know that inner ruler who rules this world, the other world and all beings from within? Patañcala Kāpya said: I do not know him, revered sir. He said to Patañcala Kāpya and to those who studied the sacrifice: Kāpya, he who knows that thread and that inner ruler is a knower of Brahman, a knower of the worlds, a knower of the gods, a knower of the Vedas, a knower of beings, a knower of the Self, a knower of all.
