He told it to them. That I know. If you, Yājñavalkya, without knowing that thread and that inner ruler, drive away the cows that belong to the knower of Brahman, your head will fall off. Yājñavalkya said: I do know, Gautama, that thread and that inner ruler. Uddālaka said: Anyone at all might say: I know, I know. Tell it as you know it. ॥3.7.1॥
3.7.2: Yājñavalkya said: Vāyu, the air, Gautama, is that thread. By Vāyu as the thread, Gautama, this world, the other world and all beings are strung together. Therefore, Gautama, of a man who has died they say: His limbs have come loose; for by Vāyu as the thread, Gautama, they are strung together. Uddālaka said: So it is, Yājñavalkya. Now speak of the inner ruler. ॥3.7.2॥
3.7.3: Yājñavalkya said: He who dwells in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, of whom the earth is the body, who rules the earth from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.3॥
Śaṅkara: the earth here is the deity of the earth, who does not know that another dwells in her; the inner ruler is the Lord, called Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all beings.
3.7.4: He who dwells in the waters, is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, of whom the waters are the body, who rules the waters from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.4॥
3.7.5: He who dwells in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, of whom fire is the body, who rules fire from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.5॥
3.7.6: He who dwells in the mid-region, is within the mid-region, whom the mid-region does not know, of whom the mid-region is the body, who rules the mid-region from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.6॥
3.7.7: He who dwells in the air, is within the air, whom the air does not know, of whom the air is the body, who rules the air from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.7॥
3.7.8: He who dwells in heaven, is within heaven, whom heaven does not know, of whom heaven is the body, who rules heaven from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.8॥
3.7.9: He who dwells in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, of whom the sun is the body, who rules the sun from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.9॥
3.7.10: He who dwells in the quarters, is within the quarters, whom the quarters do not know, of whom the quarters are the body, who rules the quarters from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.10॥
3.7.11: He who dwells in the moon and the stars, is within the moon and the stars, whom the moon and the stars do not know, of whom the moon and the stars are the body, who rules the moon and the stars from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.11॥
3.7.12: He who dwells in space, is within space, whom space does not know, of whom space is the body, who rules space from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.12॥
3.7.13: He who dwells in darkness, is within darkness, whom darkness does not know, of whom darkness is the body, who rules darkness from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.13॥
3.7.14: He who dwells in light, is within light, whom light does not know, of whom light is the body, who rules light from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. This is with regard to the deities. Now with regard to beings. ॥3.7.14॥
3.7.15: He who dwells in all beings, is within all beings, whom all beings do not know, of whom all beings are the body, who rules all beings from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. This is with regard to beings. Now with regard to the body. ॥3.7.15॥
3.7.16: He who dwells in prāṇa, is within prāṇa, whom prāṇa does not know, of whom prāṇa is the body, who rules prāṇa from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.16॥
Śaṅkara: prāṇa here is the organ of smell together with the breath.
3.7.17: He who dwells in speech, is within speech, whom speech does not know, of whom speech is the body, who rules speech from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.17॥
3.7.18: He who dwells in the eye, is within the eye, whom the eye does not know, of whom the eye is the body, who rules the eye from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.18॥
3.7.19: He who dwells in the ear, is within the ear, whom the ear does not know, of whom the ear is the body, who rules the ear from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.19॥
3.7.20: He who dwells in the mind, is within the mind, whom the mind does not know, of whom the mind is the body, who rules the mind from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.20॥
3.7.21: He who dwells in the skin, is within the skin, whom the skin does not know, of whom the skin is the body, who rules the skin from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.21॥
3.7.22: He who dwells in the intellect (vijñāna), is within the intellect, whom the intellect does not know, of whom the intellect is the body, who rules the intellect from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. ॥3.7.22॥
3.7.23: He who dwells in semen, is within semen, whom semen does not know, of whom semen is the body, who rules semen from within, he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal: unseen, he is the seer; unheard, the hearer; unthought, the thinker; unknown, the knower. There is no other seer than he, no other hearer than he, no other thinker than he, no other knower than he. He is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. What is other than this is afflicted. Thereupon Uddālaka Āruṇi fell silent. ॥3.7.23॥
Śaṅkara: semen (retas) here is the organ of generation.
3.8.1: Then Vācaknavī (Gārgī) said: Revered brāhmaṇas, well then, I shall ask him two questions. If he answers them for me, none of you will ever defeat him in a debate about Brahman (brahmodya). The brāhmaṇas said: Ask, Gārgī. ॥3.8.1॥
3.8.2: Gārgī said: Yājñavalkya, as a hero's son of Kāśī or of Videha would string his unstrung bow, take in his hand two reed-tipped arrows that pierce the foe through, and rise up to face him, just so have I risen to face you with two questions. Answer me these two. Yājñavalkya said: Ask, Gārgī. ॥3.8.2॥
3.8.3: Gārgī said: Yājñavalkya, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between them, these two, heaven and earth, themselves, and what they call the past, the present and the future: in what is that woven, warp and woof? ॥3.8.3॥
Śaṅkara: all that she names is the Sūtra spoken of earlier, in which the whole world of duality becomes one; her question is in what the Sūtra itself is woven.
3.8.4: Yājñavalkya said: Gārgī, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between them, these two, heaven and earth, themselves, and what they call the past, the present and the future: that is woven, warp and woof, in space. ॥3.8.4॥
Śaṅkara: this space is the unmanifested (avyākṛta), in which the manifested world, the Sūtra, abides in all three times: at its origin, while it lasts, and at its dissolution.
3.8.5: Gārgī said: Salutation to you, Yājñavalkya, for you have resolved this question of mine. Brace yourself for the next. Yājñavalkya said: Ask, Gārgī. ॥3.8.5॥
3.8.6: Gārgī said: Yājñavalkya, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between them, these two, heaven and earth, themselves, and what they call the past, the present and the future: in what is that woven, warp and woof? ॥3.8.6॥
3.8.7: Yājñavalkya said: Gārgī, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between them, these two, heaven and earth, themselves, and what they call the past, the present and the future: that is woven, warp and woof, in space alone. Gārgī asked: In what, then, is space woven, warp and woof? ॥3.8.7॥
3.8.8: Yājñavalkya said: This, Gārgī, is that Imperishable (akṣara) of which the brāhmaṇas, the knowers of Brahman, speak: it is not gross, not fine, not short, not long, not red, not moist; it is without shadow, without darkness, without air, without space, clinging to nothing; it has no taste, no smell, no eyes, no ears, no speech, no mind, no radiance, no prāṇa (the vital breath), no mouth, no measure; it has no inside and no outside; it eats nothing, and nothing eats it. ॥3.8.8॥
3.8.9: Under the rule (praśāsana) of this Imperishable, Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held in their places; under the rule of this Imperishable, Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held in their places; under the rule of this Imperishable, Gārgī, the moments, the muhūrtas, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons and years stand held in their places; under the rule of this Imperishable, Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward from the white mountains, others westward, and others in whatever direction (each takes); under the rule of this Imperishable, Gārgī, men praise those who give, the gods depend on the sacrificer, and the ancestors on the darvī offering. ॥3.8.9॥
3.8.10: Whoever, Gārgī, without knowing this Imperishable, makes offerings in this world, sacrifices and practises austerity for many thousands of years, all that of his comes to an end; whoever, Gārgī, departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is to be pitied (kṛpaṇa); but he who departs from this world knowing this Imperishable, Gārgī, is a brāhmaṇa. ॥3.8.10॥
3.8.11: That Imperishable, Gārgī, unseen, is the seer; unheard, the hearer; unthought, the thinker; unknown, the knower. There is no other seer than it, no other hearer than it, no other thinker than it, no other knower than it. In this Imperishable, Gārgī, is space woven, warp and woof. ॥3.8.11॥
3.8.12: Gārgī said: Revered brāhmaṇas, count it a great thing if you get free of him by bowing to him; none of you will ever defeat him in a debate about Brahman. Thereupon Vācaknavī fell silent. ॥3.8.12॥
3.9.1: Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there? Yājñavalkya answered with this very nivid: As many as are named in the nivid of the Vaiśvadeva (śastra): three and three hundred, three and three thousand. Śākalya said: Om (yes). Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: Thirty-three. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: Six. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: Three. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: Two. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: One and a half. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there in fact? Yājñavalkya said: One. Śākalya said: Om. Śākalya asked: Which are those three and three hundred, three and three thousand? ॥3.9.1॥
Śaṅkara: the nivid is a set of mantra words, recited in the Vaiśvadeva śastra, that state the number of the gods.
3.9.2: Yājñavalkya said: These are only their glories (mahiman); the gods are only thirty-three. Śākalya asked: Which are those thirty-three? Yājñavalkya said: The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas: these make thirty-one; and Indra and Prajāpati make up the thirty-three. ॥3.9.2॥
3.9.3: Śākalya asked: Which are the Vasus? Yājñavalkya said: Fire and earth, air and the mid-region, the sun and heaven, the moon and the stars: they are the Vasus, since in them all this is placed to dwell (vasu); therefore they are the Vasus. ॥3.9.3॥
Śaṅkara: as the support of the fruit of beings' karma, and turning into their bodies and organs, they make all this world dwell (vāsayanti) and themselves dwell in it; hence they are Vasus.
3.9.4: Śākalya asked: Which are the Rudras? Yājñavalkya said: These ten prāṇas (the organs) in a man, the eleventh being the self (ātman). When they go out of this mortal body, they make (his kin) weep; because they make them weep, they are the Rudras. ॥3.9.4॥
Śaṅkara: the ten prāṇas are the organs of action and of knowledge, and the self that is the eleventh is the mind.
3.9.5: Śākalya asked: Which are the Ādityas? Yājñavalkya said: The twelve months of the year are the Ādityas, for they move on, taking up all this; because they move on taking up (ādadānāḥ) all this, they are the Ādityas. ॥3.9.5॥
3.9.6: Śākalya asked: Which is Indra, which is Prajāpati? Yājñavalkya said: The thunder (stanayitnu) is Indra, the sacrifice is Prajāpati. Śākalya asked: Which is the thunder? Yājñavalkya said: The thunderbolt (aśani). Śākalya asked: Which is the sacrifice? Yājñavalkya said: The animals. ॥3.9.6॥
3.9.7: Śākalya asked: Which are the six? Yājñavalkya said: Fire and earth, air and the mid-region, the sun and heaven: these are the six, for all this is these six. ॥3.9.7॥
3.9.8: Śākalya asked: Which are the three gods? Yājñavalkya said: These three worlds, for all these gods are in them. Śākalya asked: Which are the two gods? Yājñavalkya said: Food and prāṇa, the vital breath. Śākalya asked: Which is the one and a half? Yājñavalkya said: He who blows here (the wind). ॥3.9.8॥
Śaṅkara: each world together with its god is one god, the earth with fire, the mid-region with air, heaven with the sun; he gives this as the view of some etymologists (Nairuktas).
3.9.9: On this they say: he blows as though he were one only; how, then, is he one and a half? Because in him all this grew to greatness (adhyārdhnot), therefore he is the one and a half (adhyardha). Śākalya asked: Which is the one god? Yājñavalkya said: Prāṇa. He is Brahman; they call him the beyond (tyat). ॥3.9.9॥
Śaṅkara: prāṇa is the great Brahman because all the gods are its own self; tyat is a word that names what is remote.
3.9.10: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is the earth alone, whose loka (means of seeing) is fire, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person who dwells in the body (śārīra). Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: The immortal (amṛta). ॥3.9.10॥

Śaṅkara: loka is that by which he sees, and the whole self is the body with its organs; deity here is that from which each person arises, and the immortal is the essence of eaten food, from which the mother's blood is formed.
3.9.11: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is desire alone, whose loka is the heart, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person made of desire. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Women. ॥3.9.11॥
3.9.12: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is forms alone, whose loka is the eye, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is that very person in the sun. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Truth (satya). ॥3.9.12॥
Śaṅkara: truth here means the eye, for the sun among the gods arises from the eye within the body.
3.9.13: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is space alone, whose loka is the ear, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person who is in the ear and present at each hearing (prātiśrutka). Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: The quarters. ॥3.9.13॥
3.9.14: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is darkness alone, whose loka is the heart, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person made of shadow. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Death. ॥3.9.14॥
Śaṅkara: darkness here is the darkness of night and the like; within the body, the person made of shadow is the person made of ignorance, and death is the deity from which he arises.
3.9.15: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is forms alone, whose loka is the eye, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person in the mirror. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Life (asu). ॥3.9.15॥
Śaṅkara: forms in general were spoken of before (3.9.12), here bright, shining forms; the mirror and the like hold the reflection, and this person, the reflection, arises from asu, that is, prāṇa.
3.9.16: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is the waters alone, whose loka is the heart, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person in the waters. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Varuṇa. ॥3.9.16॥
3.9.17: Śākalya said: The person whose abode is semen alone, whose loka is the heart, whose light is the mind, the final support of the whole self: he who knows that person would indeed be a knower, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: I do know that person, the final support of the whole self, of whom you speak: it is this very person made of the son. Ask on, Śākalya. Śākalya asked: Who is his deity? Yājñavalkya said: Prajāpati. ॥3.9.17॥
Śaṅkara: Prajāpati here is the father, for the son is born of the father.
3.9.18: Yājñavalkya said: Śākalya, have these brāhmaṇas, I wonder, made you their tongs for the burning coals? ॥3.9.18॥
Śaṅkara: the aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa is the tongs or the like, in which burning coals die down: the brāhmaṇas have surely made Śākalya that, and he does not see that Yājñavalkya is burning him.
3.9.19: Śākalya said: Yājñavalkya, you have belittled the brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and the Pañcālas: what Brahman do you know, that you do so? Yājñavalkya said: I know the quarters with their gods and their supports. Śākalya said: If you know the quarters with their gods and their supports, ॥3.9.19॥
3.9.20: What is your deity in this eastern quarter? Yājñavalkya said: The sun (Āditya) is my deity. Śākalya asked: In what is that sun supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the eye. Śākalya asked: And in what is the eye supported? Yājñavalkya said: In forms, for it is with the eye that one sees forms. Śākalya asked: And in what are forms supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the heart, for it is with the heart that one knows forms; in the heart alone are forms supported. Śākalya said: Just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥3.9.20॥

Śaṅkara: Yājñavalkya has realised his heart as his self spread out in five parts in the quarters, so Śākalya asks which deity is his in each quarter; the heart names the intellect and the mind together.
3.9.21: Śākalya asked: What is your deity in this southern quarter? Yājñavalkya said: Yama is my deity. Śākalya asked: In what is that Yama supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the sacrifice. Śākalya asked: And in what is the sacrifice supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the priests' fee (dakṣiṇā). Śākalya asked: And in what is the fee supported? Yājñavalkya said: In faith (śraddhā), for only when a man has faith does he give the fee; in faith alone is the fee supported. Śākalya asked: And in what is faith supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the heart, for it is with the heart that one knows faith; in the heart alone is faith supported. Śākalya said: Just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥3.9.21॥
3.9.22: Śākalya asked: What is your deity in this western quarter? Yājñavalkya said: Varuṇa is my deity. Śākalya asked: In what is that Varuṇa supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the waters. Śākalya asked: And in what are the waters supported? Yājñavalkya said: In semen. Śākalya asked: And in what is semen supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the heart. That is why, of a son born in his father's likeness, people say: He has, as it were, slipped out of his heart; he is, as it were, made from his heart; for in the heart alone is semen supported. Śākalya said: Just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥3.9.22॥
3.9.23: Śākalya asked: What is your deity in this northern quarter? Yājñavalkya said: Soma is my deity. Śākalya asked: In what is that Soma supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the consecration (dīkṣā). Śākalya asked: And in what is the consecration supported? Yājñavalkya said: In truth. That is why they say to one who has been consecrated: Speak the truth; for in truth alone is the consecration supported. Śākalya asked: And in what is truth supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the heart, for it is with the heart that one knows truth; in the heart alone is truth supported. Śākalya said: Just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥3.9.23॥
3.9.24: Śākalya asked: What is your deity in this fixed quarter (dhruvā)? Yājñavalkya said: Agni, fire, is my deity. Śākalya asked: In what is that Agni supported? Yājñavalkya said: In speech. Śākalya asked: And in what is speech supported? Yājñavalkya said: In the heart. Śākalya asked: And in what is the heart supported? ॥3.9.24॥

Śaṅkara: the fixed quarter is the upper one, which never changes for those who live all round Meru; light abounds above, and light is fire. All forms, works and names come to rest in the heart, and so the question now is about the heart that is all.
3.9.25: Yājñavalkya said: Ahallika, when you think that this (heart) is somewhere other than in us, for if it were somewhere other than in us, dogs would eat it (the body) or birds would tear it apart. ॥3.9.25॥
Śaṅkara: Ahallika is Śākalya addressed by another name; the sense is that the heart is supported in me, that is, in the body.
3.9.26: Śākalya asked: In what are you (the body) and your self supported? Yājñavalkya said: In prāṇa. Śākalya asked: And in what is prāṇa supported? Yājñavalkya said: In apāna. Śākalya asked: And in what is apāna supported? Yājñavalkya said: In vyāna. Śākalya asked: And in what is vyāna supported? Yājñavalkya said: In udāna. Śākalya asked: And in what is udāna supported? Yājñavalkya said: In samāna. This Self is the one spoken of as not thus, not thus (neti neti). He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped; undecaying, for he does not decay; unattached, for he does not cling; he is unbound, he does not suffer, he is not hurt. These are the eight abodes, the eight lokas, the eight deities, the eight persons. He who set out those persons apart, drew them back and passed beyond them: about that person taught in the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣada) I ask you. If you do not explain him to me, your head will fall off. Śākalya did not know him, and his head fell off; and robbers carried away even his bones, taking them for something else. ॥3.9.26॥
Śaṅkara: you here is the body and the self is the heart; prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna are the five functions of prāṇa, each held in place by the next.

Śaṅkara: the description as not thus, not thus is the śruti's own, out of the story's order; the eight abodes, lokas, deities and persons are those named from 3.9.10 on; his pupils were carrying the bones home for the funeral rites.
3.9.27: Then Yājñavalkya said: Revered brāhmaṇas, let whoever of you wishes question me, or let all of you question me; or whoever of you wishes, I will question him, or I will question all of you. Those brāhmaṇas did not dare. ॥3.9.27॥
3.9.28: Yājñavalkya questioned them with these verses: As a tree, the lord of the forest, so truly is a man: his hairs are its leaves, his skin its outer bark. From his skin his blood flows out, from its bark its sap; so from him, when he is wounded, it comes forth as sap does from a tree that is struck. His flesh is its pieces of wood (śakara), his sinews its inner bark (kināṭa), which is firm. His bones within are its wood; his marrow is made like its marrow. If a tree, when it is cut down, grows again from its root, newer than before, from what root, then, does a mortal grow when death has cut him down? Do not say: From semen; for that is produced from the living. A tree springs also from the seed, and when it has died it comes into being again directly. If they were to tear the tree out with its root, it would not come into being again. From what root, then, does a mortal grow when death has cut him down? If you say he is born already: no, he is born again; who, then, would bring him forth again? Brahman is consciousness and bliss, the final goal of the giver of wealth, and of him who stands firm in it and knows it. ॥3.9.28॥

Śaṅkara: Yājñavalkya's question is who brings forth again the man who has died; the brāhmaṇas did not know that root of the world, and so he won; the last sentence (Brahman is consciousness and bliss …) is the śruti's own answer, and the giver of wealth is the sacrificer who performs rites. Another well-known reading: once born, he is not born again.
4.1.1: Om. Janaka Vaideha was seated, giving audience. Then Yājñavalkya came to him. Janaka said to him: Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come: wanting cattle, or subtle questions (aṇvanta)? Yājñavalkya said: Both, O emperor. ॥4.1.1॥
4.1.2: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Jitvan Śailini told me: Speech is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Śailini said that speech is Brahman, for what could one have who does not speak? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: Speech itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as intelligence (prajñā). Janaka asked: What is its intelligence, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: Speech itself, O emperor. It is by speech, O emperor, that a kinsman is known; the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, the itihāsas, the purāṇas, the sciences (vidyā), the Upaniṣads, the verses (ślokas), the aphorisms (sūtras), the glosses (anuvyākhyānas) and the commentaries (vyākhyānas), what is sacrificed, what is offered in the fire, what is given to eat and what is given to drink, this world and the other world, and all beings are known by speech alone, O emperor. Speech, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. Speech does not leave him; all beings flow towards him (with offerings). He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.2॥

Śaṅkara: one who has a mother, a father and a teacher is one rightly taught in turn by his mother, his father and, from investiture to the end of his studies, his teacher; speech here means the deity of speech.

Śaṅkara: the abode is the body, here the organ of speech; the support is space, the unmanifested (avyākṛta), on which it rests in all three times; and prajñā is the fourth foot of Brahman, its secret name (upaniṣad): without these Brahman has one foot only, and its worship bears no fruit. What is sacrificed and the rest mean the merit that comes of sacrifice, oblation, and gifts of food and drink.
4.1.3: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Udaṅka Śaulbāyana told me: Prāṇa, the vital breath, is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Śaulbāyana said that prāṇa is Brahman, for what could one have who does not breathe? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: Prāṇa itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as the dear (priya). Janaka asked: What is its dearness, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: Prāṇa itself, O emperor. For the sake of prāṇa, O emperor, a man officiates at the sacrifice of one for whom he should not, and accepts gifts from one from whom he should not; and in whatever quarter he goes, there is fear of being killed: all for the sake of prāṇa, O emperor. Prāṇa, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. Prāṇa does not leave him; all beings flow towards him. He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.3॥
4.1.4: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Barku Vārṣṇa told me: The eye is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Vārṣṇa said that the eye is Brahman, for what could one have who does not see? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: The eye itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as truth (satya). Janaka asked: What is its truth, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: The eye itself, O emperor. To one who sees with his eye, O emperor, people say: Did you see? He says: I saw; and that is truth. The eye, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. The eye does not leave him; all beings flow towards him. He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.4॥
4.1.5: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja told me: The ear is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Bhāradvāja said that the ear is Brahman, for what could one have who does not hear? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: The ear itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as the endless (ananta). Janaka asked: What is its endlessness, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: The quarters themselves, O emperor. That is why, O emperor, to whatever quarter a man goes, he never reaches its end, for the quarters are endless. The quarters, O emperor, are the ear; the ear in turn, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. The ear does not leave him; all beings flow towards him. He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.5॥
4.1.6: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Satyakāma Jābāla told me: The mind is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Jābāla said that the mind is Brahman, for what could one have who has no mind? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: The mind itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as bliss (ānanda). Janaka asked: What is its bliss, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: The mind itself, O emperor. It is by the mind, O emperor, that a man is drawn to a woman; a son like him is born of her; he is bliss. The mind, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. The mind does not leave him; all beings flow towards him. He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.6॥
4.1.7: Yājñavalkya said: Let us hear whatever anyone has told you. Janaka said: Vidagdha Śākalya told me: The heart is Brahman. Yājñavalkya said: As one taught by a mother, a father and a teacher would say it, so Śākalya said that the heart is Brahman, for what could one have who has no heart? But did he tell you its abode and its support? Janaka said: He did not tell me. Yājñavalkya said: Then this (Brahman) has only one foot, O emperor. Janaka said: Then you tell us, Yājñavalkya. Yājñavalkya said: The heart itself is its abode, space its support; one should worship it as stability (sthiti). Janaka asked: What is its stability, Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya said: The heart itself, O emperor. The heart, O emperor, is all beings' abode; the heart, O emperor, is all beings' support, for in the heart alone, O emperor, all beings are supported. The heart, O emperor, is the highest Brahman. The heart does not leave him; all beings flow towards him. He who, knowing thus, worships it becomes a god and goes to the gods. Janaka Vaideha said: I give a thousand cows with an elephant-like bull. Yājñavalkya said: My father held that one should not take (wealth from a pupil) without having fully instructed him. ॥4.1.7॥
4.2.1: Janaka Vaideha came down from his seat (kūrca), approached him and said: Salutation to you, Yājñavalkya; instruct me. Yājñavalkya said: As a man about to go on a long journey, O emperor, would take a chariot or a boat, so your mind is well furnished with these secret names (upaniṣads); being thus eminent and wealthy, having studied the Vedas and been taught the upaniṣads, where will you go when you are released from here? Janaka said: I do not know, revered sir, where I shall go. Yājñavalkya said: Then I will tell you where you will go. Janaka said: Let the revered one tell me. ॥4.2.1॥
Śaṅkara: the upaniṣads here are the secret names (prajñā, priya and the rest) under which Brahman was to be worshipped in the brāhmaṇa before; released from here means from this body.
4.2.2: Yājñavalkya said: This person who is in the right eye is named Indha; him, who is Indha, they call Indra, indirectly, for the gods are fond, as it were, of the indirect and dislike the direct. ॥4.2.2॥

Śaṅkara: this is the person within the sun, of whom it was said before (4.1.4) that the eye is Brahman, and who dwells especially in the right eye; he is named Indha from his shining; knowing him, Janaka has become that self, Vaiśvānara.
4.2.3: Now this form of a person in the left eye is his wife, Virāj. Their meeting place (saṃstāva) is the space within the heart; their food is the red lump within the heart; their covering is the network, as it were, within the heart; and their path for going about is the channel (nāḍī) that rises upward from the heart. Like a hair split a thousandfold are these channels of his, called hitā, which are set within the heart; through them this (essence of food) flows on; therefore this one (the subtle self) is, as it were, a feeder on finer food than the bodily self. ॥4.2.3॥

Śaṅkara: Indra is the enjoyer and his wife Virāj the food he enjoys; in dream the two unite in the heart; the red lump is the finest essence of eaten food, which sustains the subtle self (taijasa), nourished on finer food than Vaiśvānara, the self of the gross body.
4.2.4: For him the eastern quarter is the eastward prāṇas, the vital breaths; the southern quarter the southward prāṇas; the western quarter the westward prāṇas; the northern quarter the northward prāṇas; the upper quarter the upward prāṇas; the lower quarter the downward prāṇas; all the quarters all the prāṇas. This Self is the one spoken of as not thus, not thus (neti neti). He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped; undecaying, for he does not decay; unattached, for he does not cling; he is unbound, he does not suffer, he is not hurt. Yājñavalkya said: Janaka, you have reached freedom from fear (abhaya). Janaka Vaideha said: May freedom from fear come to you too, Yājñavalkya, revered sir, you who make us know freedom from fear. Salutation to you. Here are the Videhas, and here I am. ॥4.2.4॥

Śaṅkara: the knower passes in turn from Vaiśvānara to the subtle self, then to the heart, then to prāṇa, the self of all, withdraws that into the inner self and reaches the fourth (turīya), the self described as not thus, not thus; at the end Janaka offers Yājñavalkya the kingdom of the Videhas and himself as his servant.
4.3.1: Yājñavalkya went to Janaka Vaideha, thinking: I will not speak. But once, when Janaka Vaideha and Yājñavalkya had talked together about the Agnihotra, the daily fire offering, Yājñavalkya had given him a boon. Janaka had chosen the boon of asking questions as he wished. Yājñavalkya had granted it to him. So it was the emperor who questioned him first. ॥4.3.1॥

Śaṅkara: Yājñavalkya came resolved to say nothing to the king; but earlier, pleased with Janaka's knowledge of the Agnihotra, he had given him a boon, and by virtue of it Janaka questioned him first, though he kept silent.
4.3.2: Janaka asked: Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have? Yājñavalkya said: He has the sun for his light, O emperor; it is by the sun as his light that he sits, goes about, does his work and comes back. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥4.3.2॥
4.3.3: Janaka asked: When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have? Yājñavalkya said: The moon is his light; it is by the moon as his light that he sits, goes about, does his work and comes back. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥4.3.3॥
4.3.4: Janaka asked: When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what light does this person have? Yājñavalkya said: Fire is his light; it is by fire as his light that he sits, goes about, does his work and comes back. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥4.3.4॥
4.3.5: Janaka asked: When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have? Yājñavalkya said: Speech is his light; it is by speech as his light that he sits, goes about, does his work and comes back. That is why, O emperor, even where one cannot make out one's own hand, one goes straight to the place where a voice is raised. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. ॥4.3.5॥
Śaṅkara: speech here means any sound (a dog barking, an ass braying), and it stands also for smell and the other objects of the senses.
4.3.6: Janaka asked: When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does this person have? Yājñavalkya said: The self (ātman) is his light; it is by the self as his light that he sits, goes about, does his work and comes back. ॥4.3.6॥
4.3.7: Janaka asked: Which is the self? Yājñavalkya said: It is this person, made of knowledge (vijñānamaya) among the prāṇas (the organs), the light within the heart. Being like (the intellect), he moves through both worlds. He seems to meditate, he seems to move about; for, having become dream, he passes beyond this world, beyond the forms of death. ॥4.3.7॥

Śaṅkara: the prāṇas here are the organs, from which the self is distinct; the heart is the intellect (buddhi); the self lights up the intellect and so looks like it, as light takes on the colour it lights up; through this likeness it seems to meditate and move, not in truth. Death is action and ignorance, and its forms are the body and the organs.
4.3.8: This person, when he is born and takes on a body, is joined with evils (pāpman). When he departs, dying, he leaves the evils behind. ॥4.3.8॥
4.3.9: This person has just two states: this one and the state of the other world. The third, the state of dream, is the junction between them; standing in that junction, he sees both these states, this one and the state of the other world. Whatever footing (ākrama) he has towards the state of the other world, taking that footing he sees both evils and joys. When he falls asleep, he takes a portion (mātrā) of this all-holding world, himself lays (the body) low, himself builds (a dream body), and sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light. Here this person is his own light. ॥4.3.9॥
4.3.10: There are no chariots there, no teams to draw them, no roads; but he makes chariots, teams and roads. There are no joys there, no delights, no great delights; but he makes joys, delights and great delights. There are no ponds there, no pools, no rivers; but he makes ponds, pools and rivers, for he is the maker. ॥4.3.10॥
4.3.11: On this there are these verses: Striking down the body through dream, himself not sleeping, he looks upon the sleeping (all things, present only as impressions). Taking the bright (light of the senses), he comes back again to his place: the golden person, the lone swan. ॥4.3.11॥

Śaṅkara: the sleeping are all things, outer and inner, withdrawn from their own forms and risen in the mind only as impressions; the bright is the pure, luminous essence of the senses; the lone swan (ekahaṃsa) is he who goes alone through waking and dream, this world and the next.
4.3.12: Guarding his lowly nest (the body) by prāṇa, the vital breath, the immortal one roams outside the nest; immortal, he goes wherever he wishes: the golden person, the lone swan. ॥4.3.12॥
4.3.13: In dream, going to high and low states, the shining one (deva) makes many forms. Now he seems to delight with women and to laugh, now he seems to see fearful things. ॥4.3.13॥
4.3.14: All see his play; no one sees him. They say: One should not wake him suddenly. If this (self) does not find its way back to its place, the body becomes hard to cure. And some say: This (dream) is only his waking state, for the things he sees awake are the very things he sees asleep. Yet here this person is his own light. Janaka said: I give you, revered sir, a thousand (cows). Speak further, for my freedom. ॥4.3.14॥

Śaṅkara: it is physicians and others who say he should not be woken suddenly, for if the self does not return to the right place of the senses, blindness, deafness and the like may follow. The view that dream is only the waking state is held by others and is rejected: in dream the senses are at rest, so the light there is the self's own.
4.3.15: Yājñavalkya said: Having enjoyed himself and roamed in this deep sleep (samprasāda), and having only seen good and evil, he comes back again the way he came, to his place, to dream. Whatever he sees there does not follow him, for this person is unattached. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. I give you, revered sir, a thousand (cows). Speak further, for my freedom. ॥4.3.15॥
Śaṅkara: samprasāda is deep sleep; the enjoying and roaming take place in dream before it; he does not do good and evil but only sees their fruits, and so is not bound by them.
4.3.16: Yājñavalkya said: Having enjoyed himself and roamed in this dream, and having only seen good and evil, he comes back again the way he came, to his place, to waking. Whatever he sees there does not follow him, for this person is unattached. Janaka said: It is just so, Yājñavalkya. I give you, revered sir, a thousand (cows). Speak further, for my freedom. ॥4.3.16॥
4.3.17: Yājñavalkya said: Having enjoyed himself and roamed in this waking state, and having only seen good and evil, he comes back again the way he came, to his place, to the state of dream (svapnānta). ॥4.3.17॥
Śaṅkara takes svapnānta here first as deep sleep (samprasāda), but allows it to mean dream as well.
4.3.18: As a great fish moves by turns along both banks, the near and the far, so this person moves by turns through both these states, the state of dream and the state of waking. ॥4.3.18॥
4.3.19: As a falcon or an eagle (suparṇa), having flown about in this sky, grows weary, folds its wings and bears itself down to its nest, so this person hastens to that state where, asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream. ॥4.3.19॥
4.3.20: These are his channels called hitā, as fine as a hair split a thousandfold, and they are full of white, blue, tawny, green and red (fluid). Now when it seems that they are killing him, that they are overpowering him, that an elephant is chasing him, that he is falling into a pit, then whatever fearful thing he sees when awake he imagines here through ignorance. And when he thinks himself a god, as it were, a king, as it were, and when he thinks: I alone am all this, that is his highest world. ॥4.3.20॥

Śaṅkara: these fears are false, born of ignorance; as knowledge grows, one who when awake knows a deity or bears the impressions of kingship thinks himself in dream a god or a king, and when the knowledge that he is the self of all is complete, he thinks: I am all. This being the self of all is his highest world, liberation.
4.3.21: That indeed is his form beyond desires, free from evils, without fear. As a man in the embrace of a beloved woman knows nothing without and nothing within, so this person, in the embrace of the knowing Self (prājña), knows nothing without and nothing within. That indeed is his form in which desires are fulfilled, in which the Self is the desire, which is without desire and beyond sorrow. ॥4.3.21॥
Śaṅkara: atichandā stands for atichandam, chanda here meaning desire, not metre; the knowing self is his own supreme Self; śokāntara means free from sorrow.
4.3.22: Here a father is no father, a mother no mother, the worlds are not worlds, the gods are not gods, the Vedas are not Vedas. Here a thief is no thief, the killer of an embryo no killer of an embryo, a Cāṇḍāla no Cāṇḍāla, a Paulkasa no Paulkasa, a monk (śramaṇa) no monk, an ascetic (tāpasa) no ascetic. (This form) is untouched by good, untouched by evil, for then he has passed beyond all the sorrows of the heart. ॥4.3.22॥

Śaṅkara: here is deep sleep, in which he is free of the deeds that make these relations; the thief is one who steals a brāhmaṇa's gold; the śramaṇa is a wandering monk and the tāpasa a forest-dweller (vānaprastha); the sorrows of the heart are desires, which rest in the intellect.
4.3.23: When there he does not see, he is in truth seeing, though he does not see; for the seeing of the seer is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could see. ॥4.3.23॥

Śaṅkara: the self is the seer by its own unceasing sight, as the sun gives light by its own unceasing light; in deep sleep, one with the supreme Self, it has no organs or objects standing apart from it, and so there is no particular seeing.
4.3.24: When there he does not smell, he is in truth smelling, though he does not smell; for the smelling of the smeller is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could smell. ॥4.3.24॥
4.3.25: When there he does not taste, he is in truth tasting, though he does not taste; for the tasting of the taster is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could taste. ॥4.3.25॥
4.3.26: When there he does not speak, he is in truth speaking, though he does not speak; for the speaking of the speaker is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could speak. ॥4.3.26॥

Śaṅkara: thinking and knowing are named apart because, though they aid seeing and the rest, they work without the eye and the other organs, on things past, future and present. Seeing, hearing and the rest are not separate attributes of the self: the one light of consciousness looks divided through the organs that condition it, as clear crystal takes the colours placed beside it.
4.3.27: When there he does not hear, he is in truth hearing, though he does not hear; for the hearing of the hearer is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could hear. ॥4.3.27॥
4.3.28: When there he does not think, he is in truth thinking, though he does not think; for the thinking of the thinker is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could think of. ॥4.3.28॥
4.3.29: When there he does not touch, he is in truth touching, though he does not touch; for the touching of the toucher is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could touch. ॥4.3.29॥
4.3.30: When there he does not know, he is in truth knowing, though he does not know; for the knowing of the knower is never lost, since it is imperishable. But no second exists then, other than him and separate from him, that he could know. ॥4.3.30॥
4.3.31: Where there is, as it were, another, there one may see another, one may smell another, one may taste another, one may speak to another, one may hear another, one may think of another, one may touch another, one may know another. ॥4.3.31॥
Śaṅkara: where, in waking or in dream, ignorance sets up something as if other than the self, there one who takes himself too for another sees another.
4.3.32: He becomes (clear) as water, one, the seer, without a second. This is the world of Brahman, O emperor: thus Yājñavalkya taught him. This is his highest goal, this his highest treasure, this his highest world, this his highest bliss. Other beings live on a portion of this very bliss. ॥4.3.32॥

Śaṅkara: salila means clear as water; the world of Brahman here is Brahman itself, the world that is Brahman; the portion of this bliss that other beings enjoy reaches them through ignorance, in the contact of the senses with their objects.
4.3.33: He who among men is whole of body and prosperous, a lord over others, most richly endowed with all human enjoyments: he is the highest bliss of men. A hundred blisses of men are one bliss of the fathers who have won their world. A hundred blisses of the fathers who have won their world are one bliss in the world of the gandharvas. A hundred blisses in the world of the gandharvas are one bliss of the gods by works, who reach godhood by their works. A hundred blisses of the gods by works are one bliss of the gods by birth, and of him who is learned in the Veda (śrotriya), sinless and not struck by desire. A hundred blisses of the gods by birth are one bliss in the world of Prajāpati, and of him who is learned in the Veda, sinless and not struck by desire. A hundred blisses in the world of Prajāpati are one bliss in the world of Brahmā, and of him who is learned in the Veda, sinless and not struck by desire. And this is the highest bliss. This is the world of Brahman, O emperor, said Yājñavalkya. Janaka said: I give you, revered sir, a thousand (cows). Speak further, for my freedom. At this Yājñavalkya grew afraid: The king is intelligent; he has hemmed me in at all my conclusions. ॥4.3.33॥

Śaṅkara: in this ladder the world of Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha's; the highest bliss is that of deep sleep (samprasāda), in which these hundredfold blisses become one, and the learned man free of desire knows it directly. Learning and sinlessness are alike at every step; it is the growth of freedom from desire that raises the bliss a hundredfold.
The conclusions are the settled answers to the king's questions: Yājñavalkya feared that, by way of his boon of asking at will, the king meant to draw out all his knowledge (Śaṅkara).
4.3.34: Yājñavalkya said: Having enjoyed himself and roamed in this state of dream (svapnānta), and having only seen good and evil, he comes back again the way he came, to his place, to waking. ॥4.3.34॥
4.3.35: As a heavily laden cart goes creaking, just so this embodied self, mounted by the knowing Self (prājña), goes groaning, when he comes to breathe upward. ॥4.3.35॥
Śaṅkara: the embodied self is the self with the subtle body (liṅga) for its adjunct; it groans in pain as the vital parts are severed; it is lit by the knowing Self, and only so does it seem to go.
4.3.36: When this (body) grows thin — it grows thin through old age or through illness — then, as a mango or a fig (udumbara) or a pippala fruit comes loose from its stalk, just so this person, freeing himself wholly from these limbs, hastens back again the way he came, to a (new) birth, for prāṇa alone. ॥4.3.36॥
Śaṅkara: he goes to one birth or another according to his deeds and his learning; for prāṇa means so that the prāṇas, the organs, may unfold again in a new body.
4.3.37: As, for a king who is coming, the Ugras, the officers who punish offenders (pratyenas), the Sūtas and the village heads wait ready with food, drink and lodgings, saying: Here he comes, here he arrives; just so, for one who knows thus, all beings wait ready, saying: Here comes Brahman, here it arrives. ॥4.3.37॥

Śaṅkara: the Ugras are a caste (or men of harsh deeds) and the Sūtas a mixed caste; one who knows thus is the transmigrating self who knows the fruit of his karma, and Brahman here is that self, the enjoyer and doer, of whom they say: he is coming to us; the beings, the elements that make the body and the sun and the other deities that aid the organs, are moved by his karma and wait ready with the means of enjoying its fruit.
4.3.38: As, when a king is about to set out, the Ugras, the officers who punish offenders, the Sūtas and the village heads gather round him, just so at the time of death all the prāṇas (the organs) gather round this self, when he comes to breathe upward. ॥4.3.38॥
4.4.1: When this self comes to weakness and comes, as it were, to bewilderment, then these prāṇas (the organs) gather round him. Drawing these particles of light (tejomātrā) wholly into himself, it is into the heart that he comes down. When the person in the eye turns away and goes back, then he no longer knows forms. ॥4.4.1॥

Śaṅkara: the weakness and the bewilderment belong to the body and the organs, not to the self, hence as it were; the particles of light are the eye and the other organs; the person in the eye is a part of the sun, which at death stops aiding the eye and goes back to the sun.
4.4.2: (The organ) becomes one (with him); he does not see, they say. It becomes one; he does not smell, they say. It becomes one; he does not taste, they say. It becomes one; he does not speak, they say. It becomes one; he does not hear, they say. It becomes one; he does not think, they say. It becomes one; he does not touch, they say. It becomes one; he does not know, they say. Then the tip of his heart lights up, and by that light this self goes out, through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. As he goes out, prāṇa, the vital breath, goes out after him; as prāṇa goes out, all the prāṇas (the organs) go out after it. He comes to have particular awareness, and it is into what has awareness that he passes. Knowledge and work take hold of him and follow him, and so does his past experience (pūrvaprajñā). ॥4.4.2॥

Śaṅkara: when its deity withdraws, the organ becomes one with the subtle body (liṅga), and those beside him say: He does not see. The self goes out by the eye if his knowledge or work leads to the sun's world, by the head if to Brahmā's world. His awareness at death is ruled by his karma, not free. Past experience is the impression left by the fruits of past deeds, without which there is neither work nor its enjoyment.
4.4.3: As a leech on a blade of grass, coming to the end of the blade, takes hold of another support and draws itself over onto it, just so this self, casting down this body and making it unconscious, takes hold of another support and draws itself over onto it. ॥4.4.3॥
4.4.4: As a goldsmith, taking a piece of gold, fashions another form, newer and more beautiful, just so this self, casting down this body and making it unconscious, makes for itself another form, newer and more beautiful: that of the fathers, or of the gandharvas, or of the gods, or of Prajāpati, or of Brahmā, or of other beings. ॥4.4.4॥
Śaṅkara takes peśaskārī as a goldsmith (peśas, gold); the word can also mean a woman embroiderer.
4.4.5: This Self is indeed Brahman: made of knowledge (vijñāna), made of mind, made of prāṇa, made of the eye, made of the ear, made of earth, made of water, made of air, made of space, made of light and of what is not light, made of desire and of desirelessness, made of anger and of freedom from anger, made of dharma (right conduct) and of adharma, made of everything. This is what is meant by: he is made of this, made of that. As he acts, as he conducts himself, so he becomes. The doer of good becomes good, the doer of evil becomes evil. One becomes virtuous by virtuous work, sinful by sinful work. And some indeed say: This person is made of desire alone. As his desire is, so is his resolve (kratu); as his resolve is, so is the work he does; whatever work he does, that (its fruit) he attains. ॥4.4.5॥

Śaṅkara: made of this means made of what is being perceived, and made of that, of the unseen states within, known from what they bring about. Some say: those who know bondage and liberation, for whom desire alone is the root of worldly existence.
4.4.6: On this there is a verse: Attached, he goes with his karma, his deeds, to that very thing on which his mind, the liṅga, is set. When he has come to the end of (the fruit of) whatever work he does here, he comes back again from that world to this world, for work. So it is with the man who desires. Now the man who does not desire: he who is without desire, freed from desire, whose desires are fulfilled, whose desire is the Self — his prāṇas do not go out; being none other than Brahman, he goes to Brahman. ॥4.4.6॥

Śaṅkara: the mind is called the liṅga because it is the chief part of the subtle body, or because by it one knows; attached to the fruit, he goes to the fruit of the deeds he did with that attachment. The prāṇas of the knower do not go out; he is Brahman here itself, not after the body falls.
4.4.7: On this there is a verse: When all the desires lodged in his heart are let go, then the mortal becomes immortal; here (in this body) he attains Brahman. And just as a snake's slough lies on an anthill, dead and cast off, so this body lies. But this bodiless, immortal prāṇa is Brahman alone, is light alone. Janaka Vaideha said: I give you, revered sir, a thousand (cows). ॥4.4.7॥
Śaṅkara: prāṇa here is the supreme Self (that which breathes, the breath of the breath); the light is the light of consciousness.
4.4.8: On this there are these verses: The subtle path, wide and ancient, has reached me; I myself have found it in full. By it the wise, the knowers of Brahman, go from here upward, freed, to the heavenly world. ॥4.4.8॥

Śaṅkara: the path is that of knowledge; subtle, as it is hard to know; wide (or, reading vitara, carrying across); the heavenly world here is liberation; from here upward means after this body falls, for those already freed while living.
4.4.9: In it, they say, there is white, or blue, tawny, green and red. This path was found by the brāhmaṇa; by it goes the knower of Brahman who has done good and is full of light (taijasa). ॥4.4.9॥

Śaṅkara: some seekers call that path white, others blue and so on; but these colours are those of the channels (nāḍīs) or of the sun, which lead to Brahmā's world and the like, not to liberation. This path of knowledge was found by the brāhmaṇa who has given up all desires and is one with the supreme Self; the doer of good is one who did good before and then renounced.
4.4.10: Those who worship avidyā enter blind darkness; into darkness greater still, as it were, go those who delight in vidyā. ॥4.4.10॥

Śaṅkara here takes avidyā as ritual work, of means and ends, and vidyā as the three Vedas studied for ritual alone, by those who disregard the Upaniṣads; on the same mantra of the Īśa he takes vidyā as meditation on the deities.
4.4.11: Those worlds are called “joyless”, covered in blind darkness. People who are unlearned and unawakened go to them after death. ॥4.4.11॥
4.4.12: If a person should know the Self as: I am this — then wishing for what, and for whose desire, would he follow the body in its suffering? ॥4.4.12॥
Śaṅkara: if shows how rare the knowledge of the Self is; I am this means I am this supreme Self, the witness of all beings.
4.4.13: He who has found and awakened to the Self that has entered this deep, impenetrable body is the maker of all, for he is the doer of everything; the world is his, and he indeed is the world itself. ॥4.4.13॥
4.4.14: While we are still here, we have come to know it; had we not, I would have remained ignorant, and great would have been the destruction. Those who know it become immortal; but the others go only to sorrow. ॥4.4.14॥
4.4.15: When one directly beholds this Self, the shining one (deva), the lord of the past and the future, he no longer seeks to hide himself from him. ॥4.4.15॥
4.4.16: That on this side of which the year revolves with its days, that light of lights, the immortal, the gods worship as life. ॥4.4.16॥
4.4.17: That in which the five pañcajanas (the five kinds of beings) and space are established, that alone I regard as the Self, the immortal Brahman; knowing it, I am immortal. ॥4.4.17॥

Śaṅkara: the five pañcajanas here are the gandharvas, the ancestors (pitṛs), the gods, the demons (asuras) and the rākṣasas, or the four varṇas with the Niṣādas as the fifth; and space here is the unmanifested (avyākṛta).
4.4.18: Those who know the prāṇa of the prāṇa and the eye of the eye and the ear of the ear, and who know the mind of the mind, have known for certain the ancient, primordial Brahman. ॥4.4.18॥
4.4.19: By the (purified) mind alone is this to be seen; there is no difference here at all. He who sees as if there were difference here goes from death to death. ॥4.4.19॥
4.4.20: In one way alone is this to be seen, this immeasurable, unchanging one. The Self is stainless, beyond space, unborn, great, imperishable. ॥4.4.20॥
4.4.21: Knowing him alone, the wise brāhmaṇa should gain insight (prajñā); he should not dwell on many words, for that is a wearying of speech. ॥4.4.21॥
4.4.22: This great unborn Self is he who is made of knowledge (vijñānamaya) among the prāṇas (the organs). In the space that is within the heart he lies; he is the controller of all, the ruler of all, the sovereign of all. He does not become greater by good work, nor any less by bad work. He is the lord of all, the sovereign of beings, the protector of beings; he is the dam (setu) that holds these worlds apart, so that they do not run into one another. Him the brāhmaṇas seek to know by Vedic study, by sacrifice, by gifts, and by austerity that is a fasting from desires (anāśaka). Knowing him alone one becomes a muni, a man of meditation. Desiring him alone as their world, renunciates go forth from home. It was for this that the knowers of old did not desire offspring, thinking: What shall we do with offspring, we whose world is this Self? They rose above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds, and then went about begging alms. For the desire for sons is itself the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is itself the desire for worlds; both of these are only desires. This Self is the one spoken of as not thus, not thus (neti neti). He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped; undecaying, for he does not decay; unattached, for he does not cling; he is unbound, he does not suffer, he is not hurt. These two do not overcome him, the thought For this I did evil and the thought For this I did good; he overcomes both of them. What he has done and what he has left undone do not burn him. ॥4.4.22॥
4.4.23: This has been declared by a ṛc, a verse of the Veda: This is the eternal greatness of the brāhmaṇa (the knower of Brahman): it does not grow greater by work, nor does it become less. One should know the very nature of that (greatness); knowing it, one is not stained by evil work. Therefore he who knows thus, being calm, restrained, withdrawn, enduring and collected, sees the Self in himself; he sees all as the Self. No evil overcomes him; he overcomes all evil. No evil burns him; he burns all evil. He becomes a brāhmaṇa free from evil, free from passion (rajas), free from doubt. This is the world that is Brahman (brahmaloka), O emperor; you have been brought to it: so said Yājñavalkya. Janaka said: I give you, revered sir, the Videhas, and myself too along with them, to be your servant. ॥4.4.23॥
4.4.24: This great unborn Self is the eater of food, the giver of wealth. He who knows thus finds wealth. ॥4.4.24॥
4.4.25: This great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless; it is Brahman. Brahman indeed is fearless. He who knows thus surely becomes the fearless Brahman. ॥4.4.25॥
4.5.1: Now Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Of the two, Maitreyī was one who discoursed on Brahman (brahmavādinī); Kātyāyanī at that time had only such understanding as women commonly had, concerned with the household. Then Yājñavalkya was about to take up another way of life (renunciation). ॥4.5.1॥
4.5.2: Yājñavalkya said: Maitreyī, my dear, I am about to go forth as a renunciate from this station (the householder's life). Come, let me make a settlement between you and Kātyāyanī here (dividing what I have). ॥4.5.2॥
4.5.3: Maitreyī said: Revered sir, if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would I become immortal by it, or not? Yājñavalkya said: No. Your life would be just like the life of those who have plenty of means; but through wealth there is no hope of immortality. ॥4.5.3॥
4.5.4: Maitreyī said: What should I do with that which would not make me immortal? Tell me just what you, revered sir, know (of the way to immortality). ॥4.5.4॥
4.5.5: Yājñavalkya said: You have indeed been dear to us, and now you have made what is dear grow greater. Come then, lady, I shall explain this to you; but while I explain, meditate deeply on what I say. ॥4.5.5॥
4.5.6: Yājñavalkya said: Not for the sake of the husband, my dear, is the husband dear; the husband is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the wife, my dear, is the wife dear; the wife is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of sons, my dear, are sons dear; sons are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of wealth, my dear, is wealth dear; wealth is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of cattle, my dear, are cattle dear; cattle are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the priestly class (brahman), my dear, is the priestly class dear; the priestly class is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the ruling class (kṣatra), my dear, is the ruling class dear; the ruling class is dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the worlds, my dear, are the worlds dear; the worlds are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the gods, my dear, are the gods dear; the gods are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of the Vedas, my dear, are the Vedas dear; the Vedas are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of beings, my dear, are beings dear; beings are dear for the sake of the Self. Not for the sake of all, my dear, is all dear; all is dear for the sake of the Self. It is the Self, my dear, that is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected on, to be meditated on. Maitreyī, my dear, when the Self indeed is seen, heard, reflected on and known, all this is known. ॥4.5.6॥
4.5.7: The priestly class rejects him who knows the priestly class as other than the Self; the ruling class rejects him who knows the ruling class as other than the Self; the worlds reject him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods reject him who knows the gods as other than the Self; the Vedas reject him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self; beings reject him who knows beings as other than the Self; all rejects him who knows all as other than the Self. This priestly class, this ruling class, these worlds, these gods, these Vedas, these beings, all this, is what this Self is. ॥4.5.7॥
4.5.8: It is as with a drum being beaten: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. ॥4.5.8॥
4.5.9: It is as with a conch being blown: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the conch, or the one who blows the conch, the sound is grasped. ॥4.5.9॥
4.5.10: It is as with a vīṇā being played: one cannot grasp its sounds as things outside it, but by grasping the vīṇā, or the one who plays the vīṇā, the sound is grasped. ॥4.5.10॥
4.5.11: As from a fire laid with damp fuel clouds of smoke go forth in many ways, so, my dear, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa (the Atharvaveda), the itihāsa (histories), the purāṇa (ancient lore), the vidyās (sciences), the Upaniṣads, the ślokas (verses), the sūtras (aphorisms), the anuvyākhyānas (explanations), the vyākhyānas (commentaries), sacrifice, oblation, food given, drink given, this world and the other world, and all beings are the breathing out of this great Being; all these are breathed out by this one alone. ॥4.5.11॥
4.5.12: As the ocean is the one place where all waters meet (ekāyana), so the skin is the one meeting place of all touches, the nose of all smells, the tongue of all tastes, the eye of all forms, the ear of all sounds, the mind of all resolves, the heart of all knowledge, the two hands of all actions, the organ of generation of all joys, the anus of all excretions, the two feet of all journeys, and speech of all the Vedas. ॥4.5.12॥
4.5.13: As a lump of salt is without inside or outside, entirely a mass of taste alone, so, my dear, this Self is without inside or outside, entirely a mass of consciousness (prajñāna) alone. Arising out of these elements, it vanishes along with them; after departing (from the body) there is no consciousness (saṃjñā). This is what I say, my dear: so said Yājñavalkya. ॥4.5.13॥

Śaṅkara: when knowledge dissolves all effects, the one Self remains, like the lump of salt, without inside or outside, a mass of consciousness; its particular consciousness came from contact with the elements, and once knowledge has dissolved that particular consciousness and that contact, there is no (particular) consciousness after departing.
4.5.14: Maitreyī said: Just here, revered sir, you have brought me into the midst of bewilderment; I do not understand this (Self). Yājñavalkya said: I am not saying anything bewildering, my dear; this Self, my dear, is imperishable, by its nature never cut off. ॥4.5.14॥
4.5.15: For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another, one smells another, one tastes another, one speaks to another, one hears another, one thinks of another, one touches another, one knows another. But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then with what should one see whom, with what should one smell whom, with what should one taste whom, with what should one speak to whom, with what should one hear whom, with what should one think of whom, with what should one touch whom, with what should one know whom? By what should one know that by which one knows all this? This Self is the one spoken of as not thus, not thus (neti neti). He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped; undecaying, for he does not decay; unattached, for he does not cling; he is unbound, he does not suffer, he is not hurt. By what, my dear, should one know the knower? You have now been given the teaching, Maitreyī; this much, my dear, is indeed immortality. Having said this, Yājñavalkya went away (into the wandering life). ॥4.5.15॥
4.6.1: Now the line of teachers. Pautimāṣya received this teaching from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya, Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Kauśika, Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya, Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kauśika and from Gautama, Gautama ॥4.6.1॥
Śaṅkara: this is the line of teachers of the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa (the third and fourth adhyāyas of this Upaniṣad), as the earlier one was the Madhu-kāṇḍa's; it is to be explained as that one was.
4.6.2: from Āgniveśya, Āgniveśya from Gārgya, Gārgya from Gārgya, Gārgya from Gautama, Gautama from Saitava, Saitava from Pārāśaryāyaṇa, Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Gārgyāyaṇa, Gārgyāyaṇa from Uddālakāyana, Uddālakāyana from Jābālāyana, Jābālāyana from Mādhyandināyana, Mādhyandināyana from Saukarāyaṇa, Saukarāyaṇa from Kāṣāyaṇa, Kāṣāyaṇa from Sāyakāyana, Sāyakāyana from Kauśikāyani, Kauśikāyani ॥4.6.2॥
4.6.3: from Ghṛtakauśika, Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa, Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya, Jātūkarṇya from Āsurāyaṇa and from Yāska, Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi, Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani, Aupajandhani from Āsuri, Āsuri from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Ātreya, Ātreya from Māṇṭi, Māṇṭi from Gautama, Gautama from Gautama, Gautama from Vātsya, Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya, Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita, Kumārahārita from Gālava, Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya, Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava, Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Panthā Saubhara, Panthā Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra, Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra, Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins, the two Aśvins from Dadhyaṅ Ātharvaṇa, Dadhyaṅ Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva, Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana, Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana, Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi, Ekarṣi from Vipracitti, Vipracitti from Vyaṣṭi, Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru, Sanāru from Sanātana, Sanātana from Sanaga, Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin, Parameṣṭhin from Brahman. Brahman is self-existent. Salutation to Brahman. ॥4.6.3॥
5.1.1: Om. That (the unseen Brahman) is whole; this (the seen world) is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth. When the whole is taken from the whole, the whole alone remains. Om is Brahman, space (kha). Space is the ancient one. Space is that which holds the air: so Kauravyāyaṇīputra used to say. This (Om) is the Veda, so the brāhmaṇas know; for by it one knows what is to be known. ॥5.1.1॥

Śaṅkara: “that” is the supreme Brahman, free of all limiting adjuncts, and “this” is the same Brahman in name and form; when by knowledge one takes the wholeness of the whole (knowing: I am that whole Brahman), Brahman alone, whole, remains. The ancient space is the supreme Self; Kauravyāyaṇīputra takes kha as the space that holds the air; either way Om is the support for meditation on Brahman.
5.2.1: The three kinds of Prajāpati's offspring, the gods, men and demons (asuras), lived with their father Prajāpati as students, in brahmacarya. Having lived as students, the gods said: Speak to us, sir. To them he spoke this syllable, da, and asked: Did you understand? They said: We understood; you told us: Restrain yourselves (dāmyata). Prajāpati said: Yes (Om), you understood. ॥5.2.1॥
5.2.2: Then men said to him: Speak to us, sir. To them he spoke this same syllable, da, and asked: Did you understand? They said: We understood; you told us: Give (datta). Prajāpati said: Yes, you understood. ॥5.2.2॥
5.2.3: Then the demons said to him: Speak to us, sir. To them he spoke this same syllable, da, and asked: Did you understand? They said: We understood; you told us: Be compassionate (dayadhvam). Prajāpati said: Yes, you understood. This very thing the divine voice, the thunder, repeats: da, da, da; that is, restrain yourselves, give, be compassionate. Therefore one should learn these three: self-restraint, giving and compassion. ॥5.2.3॥
Śaṅkara: the gods are by nature unrestrained, men greedy and the demons cruel; or all three are men, called gods, men or demons by these faults; so it is men who are to learn all three.
5.3.1: This is Prajāpati: the heart. This is Brahman; this is all. Hṛdayam, the heart, is a word of three syllables. Hṛ is one syllable: his own people and others bring (offerings) to him who knows thus. Da is one syllable: his own people and others give to him who knows thus. Yam is one syllable: he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world. ॥5.3.1॥
5.4.1: That (Brahman, the heart) was indeed just this: the true (satya) itself. He who knows thus this great, adorable, first-born being, that the true is Brahman, conquers these worlds; and conquered in the same way is that one, his enemy, and he comes to nothing: he who knows thus this great, adorable, first-born being, that the true is Brahman; for the true indeed is Brahman. ॥5.4.1॥
5.5.1: In the beginning this was the waters alone. The waters brought forth the true (satya); the true is Brahman. Brahman brought forth Prajāpati, and Prajāpati the gods. Those gods worship the true alone. This word, satyam, has three syllables. Sa is one syllable, ti one syllable, yam one syllable. The first and the last syllables are the true; in the middle is the untrue. This untrue is held on both sides by the true, and so it becomes mostly the true. The untrue does not harm one who knows thus. ॥5.5.1॥
5.5.2: That true is the sun yonder: the person in this orb and the person in the right eye. Each of these two rests on the other: the one in the sun rests on the one in the eye through the rays, and the one in the eye on the one in the sun through the prāṇas. When he (who dwells in the body) is about to depart, he sees this orb quite clear, without rays; these rays no longer come back to him. ॥5.5.2॥
5.5.3: Of the person who is in this orb, bhūḥ is the head: the head is one, and this syllable is one; bhuvaḥ is the two arms: the arms are two, and these syllables are two; svaḥ is the two feet: the feet are two, and these syllables are two. His secret name (upaniṣad) is ahar. He who knows thus strikes down evil and leaves it behind. ॥5.5.3॥
5.5.4: Of the person who is in the right eye, bhūḥ is the head: the head is one, and this syllable is one; bhuvaḥ is the two arms: the arms are two, and these syllables are two; svaḥ is the two feet: the feet are two, and these syllables are two. His secret name (upaniṣad) is aham. He who knows thus strikes down evil and leaves it behind. ॥5.5.4॥
5.6.1: This person is made of mind; light is his true being. He is within the heart, the size of a grain of rice or of barley. He is the ruler of all and the overlord of all; he governs all this, whatever there is. ॥5.6.1॥
5.7.1: Lightning is Brahman, they say. Lightning (vidyut) is so called because it cuts (vidāna) through (the darkness). He who knows thus, that lightning is Brahman, cuts down the evils that beset him. For lightning indeed is Brahman. ॥5.7.1॥
5.8.1: One should worship speech as a cow. She has four teats: the utterances svāhā, vaṣaṭ, hanta and svadhā. On two of her teats, svāhā and vaṣaṭ, the gods live; on hanta, men; on svadhā, the ancestors (pitṛs). Prāṇa, the vital breath, is her bull; the mind is her calf. ॥5.8.1॥
5.9.1: This fire Vaiśvānara is the one within a person, by which the food that is eaten is digested. This is its sound, which one hears on closing one's ears. When he is about to depart, he does not hear this sound. ॥5.9.1॥
5.10.1: When a person departs from this world, he comes to the air. There it opens for him as wide as the hole of a chariot wheel; through that he climbs upward. He comes to the sun. There it opens for him as wide as the hole of a lambara (a kind of drum); through that he climbs upward. He comes to the moon.
