There it opens for him as wide as the hole of a kettledrum (dundubhi); through that he climbs upward. He comes to a world without sorrow and without cold; there he dwells for endless years. ॥5.10.1॥

Śaṅkara: this is the course of one who has practised the meditations of this section; the world is Prajāpati's, free from sorrow of the mind and from cold, the pain of the body, and he dwells there for many ages (kalpas) of Brahmā.
5.11.1: This indeed is the highest austerity: that one suffers when sick. He who knows thus wins the highest world. This indeed is the highest austerity: that, when he is dead, they carry him to the forest. He who knows thus wins the highest world. This indeed is the highest austerity: that, when he is dead, they lay him on the fire. He who knows thus wins the highest world. ॥5.11.1॥
5.12.1: Some say: Food is Brahman. That is not so, for without prāṇa, the vital breath, food rots. Some say: Prāṇa is Brahman. That is not so, for without food prāṇa dries up. But these two deities, becoming one, reach the highest state. On this, Prātṛda said to his father: What good could I do to one who knows thus, and what harm could I do him? His father, stopping him with his hand, said: Not so, Prātṛda. Who reaches the highest state by the oneness of these two? And he said this to him: vi. Food indeed is vi, for all these beings have entered into food. Ram. Prāṇa indeed is ram, for all these beings delight in prāṇa. Into him who knows thus all beings enter, and in him all beings delight. ॥5.12.1॥
5.13.1: The uktha (the chief hymn recited at the sacrifice): prāṇa, the vital breath, is the uktha, for prāṇa raises up all this. From him rises a heroic son who knows the uktha; he who knows thus wins union with the uktha (sāyujya) and a place in its world (salokatā). ॥5.13.1॥
5.13.2: The yajus: prāṇa indeed is the yajus, for in prāṇa all these beings are joined. All beings are joined to him for his pre-eminence; he who knows thus wins union with the yajus and a place in its world. ॥5.13.2॥
5.13.3: The sāman: prāṇa indeed is the sāman, for in prāṇa all these beings come together. All beings come together for him and serve his pre-eminence; he who knows thus wins union with the sāman and a place in its world. ॥5.13.3॥
5.13.4: The kṣatra (the ruling power): prāṇa indeed is the kṣatra, for prāṇa is indeed the kṣatra: prāṇa protects (trāyate) this (body) from wounds (kṣaṇitoḥ). He attains the kṣatra that needs no other to protect it; he who knows thus wins union with the kṣatra and a place in its world. ॥5.13.4॥
5.14.1: Bhūmi (earth), antarikṣa (mid-region), dyaus (heaven): these are eight syllables; and one foot of the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. This (the three worlds) is that (first foot) of hers. He who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as there is in these three worlds. ॥5.14.1॥
5.14.2: Ṛcaḥ, yajūṃṣi, sāmāni (the verses, the formulas, the chants): these are eight syllables; and one foot of the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. This (the three Vedas) is that (second foot) of hers. He who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as this threefold knowledge reaches. ॥5.14.2॥
5.14.3: Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna (the vital breaths): these are eight syllables; and one foot of the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. This (the breaths) is that (third foot) of hers. He who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as there is that breathes. Now this is her fourth (turīya), visible foot, beyond the rajas (the worlds): he who shines yonder. What is the fourth is called turīya; the visible foot, for he is seen, as it were; beyond the rajas, for he shines over all the rajas, high above each of them. He who knows this foot of hers thus shines just so, with splendour and fame. ॥5.14.3॥
5.14.4: This Gāyatrī rests on that fourth, visible foot, beyond the rajas. That (foot) rests on the true (satya). The eye indeed is the true, for the eye is indeed the true. Therefore, if two should come now disputing, one saying: I saw, the other: I heard, we would believe the one who says: I saw. That true rests on strength (bala). Prāṇa indeed is strength; it rests on prāṇa. Therefore they say: strength is mightier (ogīya) than the true. Thus this Gāyatrī rests within the body (adhyātma). She protected the gayas. The prāṇas (the organs) indeed are the gayas; she protected the prāṇas. Because she protected (tatre) the gayas, she is named Gāyatrī. That Sāvitrī which he (the teacher) teaches is this very one. She protects the prāṇas of the one to whom he teaches her. ॥5.14.4॥
5.14.5: Some teach this Sāvitrī as the anuṣṭubh (verse), saying: Speech is the anuṣṭubh; we teach that speech. One should not do so; one should teach the Gāyatrī itself as the Sāvitrī. Even if one who knows thus accepts a great deal, as it were, that is not equal to even one foot of the Gāyatrī. ॥5.14.5॥
5.14.6: If one should accept these three worlds, full (of wealth), he would reach this first foot of hers. And if one should accept as much as this threefold knowledge, he would reach this second foot of hers; and if one should accept as much as there is that breathes, he would reach this third foot of hers. But this fourth, visible foot of hers, beyond the rajas, he who shines yonder, is not to be reached by anything at all; and whence could anyone accept so much? ॥5.14.6॥
Śaṅkara: such an acceptance only matches, and uses up, the fruit of knowing that foot, and brings no further fault; no gift matches the fourth foot.
5.14.7: Her upasthāna (the worship in which one approaches her): O Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless, for you are not reached. Salutation to you, the fourth, visible foot, beyond the rajas! May so-and-so not obtain that! — so (one says) of the one he hates; or: May so-and-so's wish not prosper! That wish never prospers for him about whom one worships thus. Or: I have obtained that! ॥5.14.7॥
5.14.8: On this, Janaka Vaideha said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: Ah! You called yourself a knower of the Gāyatrī; how is it, then, that you have become an elephant and carry (burdens)? Buḍila said: For, O emperor, I did not know her mouth. Janaka said: Fire indeed is her mouth. Even if they put a great deal on the fire, it burns it all; just so one who knows thus, even if he does a great deal of evil, consumes it all and becomes pure, clean, ageless and immortal. ॥5.14.8॥
5.15.1: The face of Truth is covered by a golden vessel. O Pūṣan (the Sun, nourisher of all), uncover it, so that I, devoted to the Truth, may see it. O Pūṣan, lone seer, Yama (controller of all), Sūrya, son of Prajāpati, spread apart your rays, gather in your light. Your most blessed form I see. That Person yonder — He am I. I am immortal: let my breath go back to the air outside, and then let this body end in ashes. Om! O mind (kratu), remember, remember what has been done; O mind, remember, remember what has been done. O Agni, O god who knows the thoughts of all beings, lead us by the good path to wealth (the fruit of our deeds). Keep from us the crooked sin. We offer you salutations again and again in words. ॥5.15.1॥
These lines are Īśa 15–18. Here Śaṅkara joins “immortal” to “He am I” (I, the immortal), where in the Īśa he takes it with the air; the good path is the bright northern path, free of return.
6.1.1: Om. He who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among his own people. Prāṇa, the vital breath, is indeed the eldest and the best. He who knows thus becomes the eldest and the best among his own people, and among those too among whom he wishes to be so. ॥6.1.1॥
6.1.2: He who knows the richest (vasiṣṭhā) becomes the richest among his own people. Speech is indeed the richest. He who knows thus becomes the richest among his own people, and among those too among whom he wishes to be so. ॥6.1.2॥
6.1.3: He who knows the firm ground (pratiṣṭhā) stands firm where the way is even, stands firm where it is hard. The eye is indeed the firm ground, for it is with the eye that one stands firm both where the way is even and where it is hard. He who knows thus stands firm where the way is even, stands firm where it is hard. ॥6.1.3॥
6.1.4: For him who knows fulfilment (sampad), whatever desire he desires is fulfilled. The ear is indeed fulfilment, for it is in the ear that all these Vedas are attained. For him who knows thus, whatever desire he desires is fulfilled. ॥6.1.4॥
6.1.5: He who knows the abode (āyatana) becomes the abode of his own people, the abode of people at large. The mind is indeed the abode. He who knows thus becomes the abode of his own people, the abode of people at large. ॥6.1.5॥
6.1.6: He who knows procreation (prajāti) multiplies in offspring and cattle. Semen is indeed procreation. He who knows thus multiplies in offspring and cattle. ॥6.1.6॥
Śaṅkara takes semen here to stand for the organ of generation.
6.1.7: These prāṇas (speech and the other organs), disputing among themselves, each claiming: I am the better, went to Brahman (Prajāpati) and said: Which of us is the richest (vasiṣṭha)? Brahman said: The one of you on whose going out this body is thought the more wretched, he is the richest of you. ॥6.1.7॥
6.1.8: Speech went out. Having stayed away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the mute live, not speaking with speech, but breathing with prāṇa, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, understanding with the mind and begetting with semen, so we lived. Speech entered again. ॥6.1.8॥
6.1.9: The eye went out. Having stayed away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the blind live, not seeing with the eye, but breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, understanding with the mind and begetting with semen, so we lived. The eye entered again. ॥6.1.9॥
6.1.10: The ear went out. Having stayed away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the deaf live, not hearing with the ear, but breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, understanding with the mind and begetting with semen, so we lived. The ear entered again. ॥6.1.10॥
6.1.11: The mind went out. Having stayed away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the simple-minded live, not understanding with the mind, but breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear and begetting with semen, so we lived. The mind entered again. ॥6.1.11॥
6.1.12: Semen went out. Having stayed away a year, it came back and said: How were you able to live without me? The others said: As the impotent live, not begetting with semen, but breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear and understanding with the mind, so we lived. Semen entered again. ॥6.1.12॥
6.1.13: Then prāṇa, about to go out — as a great, fine horse from Sindhu would tear up at one stroke the pegs that tether its feet — tore up these prāṇas in the same way. They said: Revered sir, do not go out; we shall not be able to live without you. Prāṇa said: Such as I am, then, pay me tribute (bali). They said: So be it. ॥6.1.13॥
6.1.14: Speech said: In that I am the richest, in that it is you who are the richest. The eye said: In that I am the firm ground, in that it is you who are the firm ground. The ear said: In that I am fulfilment, in that it is you who are fulfilment. The mind said: In that I am the abode, in that it is you who are the abode. Semen said: In that I am procreation, in that it is you who are procreation. Prāṇa said: Such as I am, then, what will be my food, and what my clothing? They said: Whatever there is here, down to dogs, down to worms, down to insects and moths, that is your food; water is your clothing. For him who knows thus this food of ana (prāṇa), nothing he eats is other than food, nothing he accepts is other than food. Therefore the learned, versed in the Veda (śrotriyas), sip water when about to eat and sip water when they have eaten; they consider that by this they make that very food not naked. ॥6.1.14॥
Śaṅkara takes this as praise of the knowledge, not as leave to eat or accept forbidden food.
Śaṅkara reads anam, prāṇa, for annam, food: by sipping they clothe prāṇa itself, for water is its clothing.
6.2.1: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya came to the assembly of the Pañcālas. He came up to Pravāhaṇa Jaivali, who was having himself waited on. Pravāhaṇa looked up at him and said: Boy! Śvetaketu answered: Sir! Pravāhaṇa asked: Has your father taught you? Śvetaketu said: Yes. ॥6.2.1॥
6.2.2: Pravāhaṇa asked: Do you know how these creatures, as they depart, go their different ways? Śvetaketu said: No. Do you know how they come back again to this world? Again he said: No. Do you know how that world is not filled up, though many go there again and again in this way? Again he said: No. Do you know at which offering in the series, when it has been offered, the waters take on the voice of man, rise up and speak? Again he said: No. Do you know the means of reaching the path of the gods (devayāna) or the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa): by doing what people reach the path of the gods or the path of the fathers? For we have also heard the seer's word: I have heard of two paths for mortals, that of the fathers and that of the gods; by these two goes all this that moves — the two that lie between the father and the mother. Śvetaketu said: I do not know even one of these. ॥6.2.2॥
In Śaṅkara's reading the father and the mother are heaven and earth, so both paths lie within the world of birth and death.
6.2.3: Then the king invited him to stay; but the boy, paying no heed to the invitation, ran off. He came to his father and said to him: So, sir, you told us before that we had been taught! The father said: How so, my wise one? Śvetaketu said: That so-called kṣatriya (rājanyabandhu) asked me five questions, and I do not know even one of them. The father asked: Which are they? These, he said, and he quoted their opening words. ॥6.2.3॥
6.2.4: The father said: My dear, you must know this of me: whatever I knew, all of it I told you. But come, let us go there; we two shall live with him as students (brahmacārins). Śvetaketu said: You go yourself, sir. Gautama (Āruṇi) came to where Pravāhaṇa Jaivali sat (in court). The king had a seat brought for him and had water brought, and then made him the guest-offering (arghya). Pravāhaṇa said to him: We give a boon to the revered Gautama. ॥6.2.4॥
6.2.5: Gautama said: This boon you have promised me; tell me the words you spoke in the boy's presence. ॥6.2.5॥
6.2.6: Pravāhaṇa said: That, Gautama, is among the boons of the gods; ask for one of the boons of men. ॥6.2.6॥
6.2.7: Gautama said: It is well known that I have gold, cows and horses, maidservants, retinues and clothing. Do not, sir, be ungenerous to us alone with what is great, endless and boundless. Pravāhaṇa said: Then, Gautama, seek it in the proper way. Gautama said: I come to you, sir, as a pupil. With words alone, indeed, did the people of old come (to a teacher). So he stayed there, having only declared that he came as a pupil. ॥6.2.7॥
6.2.8: Pravāhaṇa said: Do not hold it against us, Gautama, just as your grandfathers did not hold it against ours. As you know, before now this knowledge has never dwelt with any brāhmaṇa; but I will tell it to you, for when you speak like this, who could turn you away? ॥6.2.8॥
6.2.9: That world yonder (heaven), O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Of this fire the sun itself is the fuel, the rays are the smoke, the day is the flame, the quarters are the embers, and the intermediate quarters are the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer faith; from that offering King Soma arises. ॥6.2.9॥
In Śaṅkara's reading, faith here is the subtle waters into which the agnihotra offerings have turned, and the gods are the sacrificer's prāṇas, become Indra and the rest.
6.2.10: Parjanya, the god of rain, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Of this fire the year itself is the fuel, the clouds are the smoke, the lightning is the flame, the thunderbolt is the embers, and the rumblings of thunder are the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer King Soma; from that offering rain arises. ॥6.2.10॥
6.2.11: This world, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Of this fire the earth itself is the fuel, fire is the smoke, the night is the flame, the moon is the embers, and the stars are the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer rain; from that offering food arises. ॥6.2.11॥
6.2.12: Man, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Of this fire the open mouth itself is the fuel, prāṇa, the vital breath, is the smoke, speech is the flame, the eye is the embers, and the ear is the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer food; from that offering semen arises. ॥6.2.12॥
6.2.13: Woman, O Gautama, is indeed a fire. Of this fire her generative organ itself is the fuel, the hair is the smoke, the vulva is the flame, what is done within is the embers, and the pleasures are the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer semen; from that offering man arises. He lives for as long as he lives; then, when he dies — ॥6.2.13॥
6.2.14: Then they carry him to the fire. For him the fire itself becomes the fire, the fuel the fuel, the smoke the smoke, the flame the flame, the embers the embers, the sparks the sparks. In this very fire the gods offer man; from that offering the man arises, shining in colour. ॥6.2.14॥
6.2.15: Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith the True (satya), pass into the flame; from the flame into the day; from the day into the fortnight of the waxing moon; from the waxing fortnight into the six months when the sun travels north; from those months into the world of the gods; from the world of the gods into the sun; from the sun into the lightning. To them, once in the lightning, a person born of the mind comes and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. In those worlds of Brahman they dwell, exalted, for vast ages. For them there is no return. ॥6.2.15॥

Śaṅkara takes those who know this thus to be householders who know the five fires, and the forest-dwellers to worship, with faith, the True, Brahman as Hiraṇyagarbha; the words can also mean “worship faith and truth”.
From the other recension's “here”, Śaṅkara takes this as no return to this world within this cycle (kalpa).
6.2.16: But those who win the worlds by sacrifice, gifts and austerity pass into the smoke; from the smoke into the night; from the night into the fortnight of the waning moon; from the waning fortnight into the six months when the sun travels south; from those months into the world of the fathers; from that world into the moon. Reaching the moon, they become food; and as (the priests) drink King Soma, making it swell and wane, so the gods there feed on them. When that (work) of theirs is spent, they pass into this very space; from space into the air; from the air into rain; from rain into the earth. On reaching the earth they become food, and are offered once more in the fire that is man; then they are born in the fire that is woman; rising up again towards the worlds, they go round and round in just this way. But those who do not know these two paths become insects and moths and whatever biting creatures there are. ॥6.2.16॥
Śaṅkara explains that the gods do not literally eat them but enjoy them as masters do their servants; “swell, wane” is not a mantra here but describes Soma being filled and drunk again and again.
6.3.1: He who desires: May I attain greatness — in the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight, having kept the upasad vow (living on milk alone) for twelve days, gathers in a cup or a bowl of udumbara wood all herbs, fruits and the rest; sweeps the ground around, smears it, sets the fire in place, strews (kuśa grass) around, prepares the ghee by the prescribed (household) procedure, and, under an asterism with a male name, sets the mantha (the herbs and fruits ground and stirred together) in the middle and offers (into the fire, saying): O Jātavedas (Agni), as many gods as are in you, who turn crosswise (against him) and destroy a man's desires, to them I offer their share; may they, satisfied, satisfy me with all desires: svāhā (the call of offering). She who lies crosswise (against him), thinking: I am the one who holds all back — you are she; you, the bringer of success, I worship with a stream of ghee. Svāhā. ॥6.3.1॥
6.3.2: Svāhā to the eldest, svāhā to the best: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (the ghee clinging to the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to prāṇa (the vital breath), svāhā to the richest (vasiṣṭhā): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to speech, svāhā to the firm ground (pratiṣṭhā): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the eye, svāhā to prosperity (sampad): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the ear, svāhā to the abode (āyatana): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the mind, svāhā to procreation (prajāti): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to semen: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. ॥6.3.2॥
6.3.3: Svāhā to Agni: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to Soma: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Bhūḥ (earth), svāhā: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Bhuvaḥ (the mid-space), svāhā: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svaḥ (heaven), svāhā: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the brahman (the priestly power): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the kṣatra (the ruling power): so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to what has been: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to what will be: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the universe: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to the all: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. Svāhā to Prajāpati: so saying he offers into the fire and pours what is left (on the ladle) into the mantha. ॥6.3.3॥
6.3.4: Then he touches it (the mantha, saying): You are moving, you are blazing, you are full, you are motionless, you are the one meeting-place (of all); you are the hiṃ that has been uttered, you are the hiṃ being uttered; you are the udgītha, you are being sung; you are the call that has been proclaimed, you are the call proclaimed in answer; you are blazing in the moist (cloud); you are pervading, you are the lord; you are food, you are light, you are the closing chant (nidhana), you are the gatherer who takes all into himself. ॥6.3.4॥
6.3.5: Then he lifts it (in its vessel, in his hand, saying): You know; we know your greatness. He is the king, the ruler, the overlord; may he make me king, ruler, overlord. ॥6.3.5॥
6.3.6: Then he sips it, saying: That excellent (radiance) of Savitṛ — The winds blow honey for him who keeps to the right (ṛta); the rivers pour honey. May the plants be sweet to us. Bhūḥ, svāhā. We meditate on the radiance of the god. Sweet be the night and the dawns; sweet be the region of the earth. Sweet be heaven, our father. Bhuvaḥ, svāhā. Who may impel our minds. Sweet be the tree to us; sweet be the sun. May the cows be sweet to us. Svaḥ, svāhā. He recites the whole Sāvitrī and all the madhumatī (honey) verses, and says: May I indeed become all this. Saying at the end: Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā, he drinks (the rest), washes his hands, and lies down behind the fire with his head to the east. At dawn he worships the sun, saying: You are the one lotus of the quarters; may I become the one lotus among men. Then, going back the way he came, he sits behind the fire and recites the line of teachers (vaṃśa). ॥6.3.6॥
6.3.7: Uddālaka Āruṇi told this (mantha) to his pupil Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. ॥6.3.7॥
6.3.8: This very (mantha) Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya told to his pupil Madhuka Paiṅgya, and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. ॥6.3.8॥
6.3.9: This very (mantha) Madhuka Paiṅgya told to his pupil Cūla Bhāgavitti, and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. ॥6.3.9॥
6.3.10: This very (mantha) Cūla Bhāgavitti told to his pupil Jānaki Āyasthūṇa, and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. ॥6.3.10॥
6.3.11: This very (mantha) Jānaki Āyasthūṇa told to his pupil Satyakāma Jābāla, and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. ॥6.3.11॥
6.3.12: This very (mantha) Satyakāma Jābāla told to his pupils, and said: Even if one were to pour it on a dry stump, branches would spring from it and leaves would sprout. One should not tell it to anyone who is neither a son nor a pupil. ॥6.3.12॥
6.3.13: Four things are of udumbara wood: the ladle of udumbara, the bowl of udumbara, the fuel of udumbara, the two stirring-rods of udumbara. There are ten kinds of grain grown in the village: rice and barley, sesame and black gram (māṣa), the millets aṇu and priyaṅgu, wheat, lentils, khalva (a bean) and khalakula (horse gram). These he grinds and steeps in curd, honey and ghee, and he offers the ghee (into the fire). ॥6.3.13॥
6.4.1: Of all these beings the earth is the essence; of the earth, the waters; of the waters, the plants; of the plants, the flowers; of the flowers, the fruits; of the fruits, man; of man, the semen. ॥6.4.1॥
6.4.2: Prajāpati thought: Come, let me make a firm ground (pratiṣṭhā) for it (the semen). He created woman. Having created her, he approached her below (in union); therefore a man should approach a woman below. From his own self he raised this pressing-stone that juts forward, his organ, and with it he united with her. ॥6.4.2॥
6.4.3: Her organ is the altar, her hair the sacred grass, her skin the hide of the soma-pressing; in the middle is the kindled fire; and those two labia are the two boards of the soma-press (adhiṣavaṇa). As great as the world of one who sacrifices with the Vājapeya is, so great is the world of him who has intercourse knowing thus; he draws to himself the merit of these women. But he who has intercourse without knowing this, women draw his merit to themselves. ॥6.4.3॥
Śaṅkara joins adhiṣavaṇe, the two boards of the soma-press, with the two labia; read otherwise, the skin is the soma-press and the two labia are the fire kindled in the middle.
6.4.4: Knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi said, knowing this, Nāka Maudgalya said, knowing this, Kumārahārita said: Many mortals, brāhmaṇas by birth alone, depart from this world bereft of virility and without merit: those who have intercourse without knowing this. Much or little, this semen may be spilled, whether one is asleep or awake. ॥6.4.4॥
6.4.5: He should touch it, or address it with these words: The semen of mine that has fallen today on the earth, that has run into the plants, into the waters, this semen I here take back. May virility come back to me, brightness again, good fortune again. May the fire and the fire-altars (dhiṣṇya) again be set each in its place. So saying, he should take it with the ring finger and the thumb and rub it between his breasts or between his brows. ॥6.4.5॥
6.4.6: And if he should see himself (his reflection) in water, he should address it with these words: In me be brightness, virility, fame, wealth, merit. She indeed is the glory (śrī) among women who has put off her soiled clothes (at the end of her monthly course); therefore, when she has put off her soiled clothes and is glorious, he should go to her and invite her. ॥6.4.6॥
6.4.7: If she will not give herself to him, he may freely buy her over (with gifts); if she still will not give herself to him, he may freely beat her with a stick or with his hand and prevail over her, saying: With virility, with glory, I take your glory from you. And she becomes without glory. ॥6.4.7॥
6.4.8: If she gives herself to him, (he says): With virility, with glory, I place glory in you. And the two of them become glorious. ॥6.4.8॥
6.4.9: She of whom he wishes: May she love me — placing his organ in her, joining mouth to mouth and touching her organ, he should repeat: From every limb you come into being; from the heart you are born. You are the essence of the limbs: as one pierced by a poisoned arrow, make this woman, so-and-so, mad for me. ॥6.4.9॥
6.4.10: And she of whom he wishes: May she not conceive — placing his organ in her and joining mouth to mouth, he should breathe out into her and then draw the breath back, saying: With virility, with semen, I take the semen back from you. And she remains without seed. ॥6.4.10॥
6.4.11: And she of whom he wishes: May she conceive — placing his organ in her and joining mouth to mouth, he should draw in the breath and then breathe out into her, saying: With virility, with semen, I place semen in you. And she becomes pregnant. ॥6.4.11॥
6.4.12: Now, if a man's wife has a lover and he hates him, he should set fire in an unbaked vessel, spread a bed of reeds in reverse order, and in that fire offer, in reverse order, these reed-tips smeared with ghee, saying: You have made an offering in my kindled fire: your prāṇa and apāna (the vital breath and the downward breath) I take from you, so-and-so. You have made an offering in my kindled fire: your sons and your cattle I take from you, so-and-so. You have made an offering in my kindled fire: your sacrifices and your good works I take from you, so-and-so. You have made an offering in my kindled fire: your hope and your expectation I take from you, so-and-so. The man cursed by a brāhmaṇa who knows this departs from this world bereft of virility and without merit. Therefore, with the wife of a śrotriya (a brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda) who knows this, one should not seek dalliance; for one who knows this becomes an enemy. ॥6.4.12॥
6.4.13: Now, when the wife of a man has her monthly course, for three days she should not drink from a bronze vessel, nor should a Śūdra man or a Śūdra woman touch her; at the end of the three nights, having bathed, she should put on new clothes, and he should have her pound rice. ॥6.4.13॥
Śaṅkara reads kaṃsena pibet: for three days she should drink from a bronze vessel.
6.4.14: He who wishes that a son of fair complexion be born to him, that he study one Veda and that he live the full span of life, should have rice boiled in milk; husband and wife should both eat it with ghee, and they are then able to beget such a son. ॥6.4.14॥
6.4.15: Now he who wishes that a son brown and tawny in colour be born to him, that he study two Vedas and that he live the full span of life, should have rice cooked with curds; husband and wife should both eat it with ghee, and they are then able to beget such a son. ॥6.4.15॥
6.4.16: Now he who wishes that a son dark in colour and with reddish eyes be born to him, that he study three Vedas and that he live the full span of life, should have rice cooked in water; husband and wife should both eat it with ghee, and they are then able to beget such a son. ॥6.4.16॥
6.4.17: Now he who wishes that a learned daughter be born to him and that she live the full span of life should have rice cooked with sesame; husband and wife should both eat it with ghee, and they are then able to beget such a daughter. ॥6.4.17॥
Śaṅkara takes the daughter's learning to be in the affairs of the household only, since he holds that she has no right to the Veda.
6.4.18: Now he who wishes that a son be born to him who is learned, renowned, one who goes into assemblies, a speaker of words that people long to hear, that he study all the Vedas and that he live the full span of life, should have rice cooked with meat; husband and wife should both eat it with ghee, and they are then able to beget such a son. The meat is to be that of a bull in its prime or of an older bull. ॥6.4.18॥
6.4.19: Then, early in the morning, having prepared the ghee by the procedure of the sthālīpāka, the rice cooked in a pot for an offering, he takes portions of the sthālīpāka and offers them, saying: To Agni svāhā (the call of offering); to Anumati svāhā; to the god Savitṛ, whose impulse is true, svāhā. Having offered them, he takes up what remains and eats it. Having eaten, he gives the rest to the other, his wife. He washes his hands, fills a vessel with water and with it sprinkles her three times, saying: Rise from here, Viśvāvasu (a gandharva); seek another, a young maiden; let the wife be joined with her husband. ॥6.4.19॥
6.4.20: Then he approaches her, saying: I am ama (prāṇa), you are sā (speech); you are sā, I am ama; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛk; I am heaven, you are the earth. Come, let us join together; let us place the seed together, to gain a male child, a son. ॥6.4.20॥
6.4.21: Then he parts her thighs, saying: Part, heaven and earth. Having placed his organ in her and joined mouth to mouth, he strokes her three times from the head downward, saying: May Viṣṇu make the womb ready; may Tvaṣṭṛ shape the forms; may Prajāpati pour in; may Dhātṛ place the embryo in you. Place the embryo, O Sinīvālī; place the embryo, O broad-tressed one. May the two Aśvins, the gods garlanded with lotuses, place the embryo in you. ॥6.4.21॥
6.4.22: There are two golden fire-sticks, with which the Aśvins churned out fire; that embryo of yours we invoke, to be born in the tenth month. As the earth holds fire in her womb, as heaven is pregnant with Indra, as the wind is the embryo of the quarters, so I place an embryo in you, so-and-so. ॥6.4.22॥
6.4.23: He sprinkles with water the woman about to give birth, saying: As the wind stirs a lotus pond on every side, even so may your embryo stir and come out together with its membrane. This pen of Indra has been made, with its bolt and its fence. O Indra, drive it out, together with the child and the afterbirth. ॥6.4.23॥
6.4.24: When the son is born, he kindles the fire, places him in his lap, mixes curds and ghee in a bronze vessel and offers portions of the curds and ghee one by one, saying: In this son may I, thriving in my own home, support a thousand. May there be no break in his line, in offspring or in cattle. Svāhā. The prāṇas, the vital breaths, that are in me I offer in you with my mind. Svāhā. Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done too little here, may Agni, who knows, the maker of the right offering, make it rightly sacrificed and well offered for us. Svāhā. ॥6.4.24॥
6.4.25: Then, putting his mouth to the child's right ear, he says three times: Speech, speech. Then he mixes curds, honey and ghee and feeds it to him with gold, directly, with nothing in between. He says: I place bhūḥ in you, I place bhuvaḥ in you, I place svaḥ in you; bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ: all I place in you. ॥6.4.25॥
6.4.26: Then he names him, saying: You are Veda. This becomes his secret name. ॥6.4.26॥
6.4.27: Then, handing the child to his mother, he puts him to the breast, saying: That breast of yours which is ever full, which brings joy, which bestows treasures, which wins wealth, which gives good gifts, by which you nourish all things worth choosing, O Sarasvatī, make it here for him to drink from. ॥6.4.27॥
6.4.28: Then he addresses the child's mother with a mantra: You are Ilā, daughter of Mitra and Varuṇa; heroic woman, she has borne a hero. Be blessed with heroes, you who have blessed us with a hero. People say of such a son: Ah, you have become greater than your father; ah, you have become greater than your grandfather. Ah, by prosperity, renown and the lustre of sacred knowledge he has reached the highest summit, he who is born as the son of a brāhmaṇa who knows thus. ॥6.4.28॥
The printed text has prāpayat, has brought (to the highest summit); the meaning follows Śaṅkara, who reads prāpat, has reached.
6.5.1: Now the line of teachers. Pautimāṣīputra received this teaching from Kātyāyanīputra, Kātyāyanīputra from Gautamīputra, Gautamīputra from Bhāradvājīputra, Bhāradvājīputra from Pārāśarīputra, Pārāśarīputra from Aupasvastīputra, Aupasvastīputra from Pārāśarīputra, Pārāśarīputra from Kātyāyanīputra, Kātyāyanīputra from Kauśikīputra, Kauśikīputra from Ālambīputra and from Vaiyāghrapadīputra, Vaiyāghrapadīputra from Kāṇvīputra and from Kāpīputra, Kāpīputra ॥6.5.1॥

Śaṅkara: this is the line of teachers of the whole teaching (pravacana); the teachers are named by their mothers because the woman has the chief place here, the subject just before being how a son of merit is born.
6.5.2: from Ātreyīputra, Ātreyīputra from Gautamīputra, Gautamīputra from Bhāradvājīputra, Bhāradvājīputra from Pārāśarīputra, Pārāśarīputra from Vātsīputra, Vātsīputra from Pārāśarīputra, Pārāśarīputra from Vārkāruṇīputra, Vārkāruṇīputra from Vārkāruṇīputra, Vārkāruṇīputra from Ārtabhāgīputra, Ārtabhāgīputra from Śauṅgīputra, Śauṅgīputra from Sāṅkṛtīputra, Sāṅkṛtīputra from Ālambāyanīputra, Ālambāyanīputra from Ālambīputra, Ālambīputra from Jāyantīputra, Jāyantīputra from Māṇḍūkāyanīputra, Māṇḍūkāyanīputra from Māṇḍūkīputra, Māṇḍūkīputra from Śāṇḍilīputra, Śāṇḍilīputra from Rāthītarīputra, Rāthītarīputra from Bhālukīputra, Bhālukīputra from the two Krauñcikīputras, the two Krauñcikīputras from Vaidabhṛtīputra, Vaidabhṛtīputra from Kārśakeyīputra, Kārśakeyīputra from Prācīnayogīputra, Prācīnayogīputra from Sāñjīvīputra, Sāñjīvīputra from Prāśnīputra Āsurivāsin, Prāśnīputra from Āsurāyaṇa, Āsurāyaṇa from Āsuri, Āsuri ॥6.5.2॥
6.5.3: from Yājñavalkya, Yājñavalkya from Uddālaka, Uddālaka from Aruṇa, Aruṇa from Upaveśi, Upaveśi from Kuśri, Kuśri from Vājaśravas, Vājaśravas from Jihvāvat Bādhyoga, Jihvāvat Bādhyoga from Asita Vārṣagaṇa, Asita Vārṣagaṇa from Harita Kaśyapa, Harita Kaśyapa from Śilpa Kaśyapa, Śilpa Kaśyapa from Kaśyapa Naidhruvi, Kaśyapa Naidhruvi from Vāc, Vāc from Ambhiṇī, Ambhiṇī from Āditya. These white Yajus formulas, which come from Āditya, are made known by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. ॥6.5.3॥
Śaṅkara: white (śukla) means unmixed with the brāhmaṇa passages, or else pure.
6.5.4: The line is the same as far as Sāñjīvīputra. Sāñjīvīputra received it from Māṇḍūkāyani, Māṇḍūkāyani from Māṇḍavya, Māṇḍavya from Kautsa, Kautsa from Māhitthi, Māhitthi from Vāmakakṣāyaṇa, Vāmakakṣāyaṇa from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Vātsya, Vātsya from Kuśri, Kuśri from Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana, Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana from Tura Kāvaṣeya, Tura Kāvaṣeya from Prajāpati, Prajāpati from Brahman. Brahman is self-existent. Salutation to Brahman. ॥6.5.4॥
Śaṅkara: Brahman here is the Veda, called pravacana, which has come down to us through the line from Prajāpati, without beginning or end, self-existent and eternal; the salutation is to that Brahman.

shanti.1: Om. That (the unseen Brahman) is whole; this (the seen world) is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth.
When the whole is taken from the whole, the whole alone remains.
1.1.1: The dawn, truly, is the head of the horse fit for sacrifice.
The sun is its eye, the wind its prāṇa (the vital breath), the fire Vaiśvānara its open mouth, and the year the body of the horse fit for sacrifice.

The sky is its back, the mid-region its belly, the earth the ground for its feet, the quarters its two flanks, the intermediate quarters its ribs, the seasons its limbs, the months and half-months its joints, days and nights its feet, the stars its bones, the clouds its flesh; the sands are the half-digested food in its stomach, the rivers its veins, the mountains its liver and lungs, the herbs and trees its hairs; the rising sun is its front half, the setting sun its hind half; when it yawns, that is the lightning; when it shakes itself, that is the thunder; when it makes water, that is the rain; sound itself is its voice. ॥1.1.1॥
1.1.2: The day arose before the horse as the mahiman, the sacrificial cup of that name; its place is the eastern sea. The night arose behind it as the mahiman; its place is the western sea. These two mahimans came into being on either side of the horse. As haya it carried the gods, as vājin the gandharvas, as arvan the demons (asuras), as aśva men. The sea alone is its bond, that in which it is bound; the sea is its source. ॥1.1.2॥
1.2.1: In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by Death, by hunger, for hunger is death. He made the mind, thinking: Let me have a self (a mind).
He moved about, worshipping. As he worshipped, the waters were born. He thought: As I worshipped, ka (water) truly came to me.
That is why the arka (the sacrificial fire) is called arka.
Ka, water or joy, truly comes to him who knows thus why the arka is called arka. ॥1.2.1॥
1.2.2: The waters, truly, are the arka. What was the cream (śara) on the waters became solid.
That became the earth. When it had been made, he (Death) grew weary. From him, wearied and heated, his radiance, his essence, came forth as fire. ॥1.2.2॥
1.2.3: He divided himself threefold: the sun as a third, the air as a third (and fire as a third).

This prāṇa, the vital breath, is divided threefold. The east is its head, and that quarter and that (the north-east and the south-east) its forelegs; the west is its tail, and that and that (the north-west and the south-west) its hind legs; the south and the north its two flanks; the sky its back, the mid-region its belly, this (earth) its chest. It rests on the waters. He who knows thus finds a firm footing wherever he goes. ॥1.2.3॥
1.2.4: He desired: Let a second self (a body) be born to me.
He, Death, who is hunger, united with speech through the mind. The seed that was there became the year. Before that there was no year.
He bore him for as long as a year lasts, and after that long a time he brought him forth.
Death opened his mouth at the newborn one (to eat him). He cried bhāṇ; that became speech. ॥1.2.4॥
1.2.5: He thought: If I kill him, I shall make less food (for myself).

With that speech and that self (the mind) he brought forth all this, whatever there is: the Ṛks, the Yajuses, the Sāmans, the metres, the sacrifices, the creatures, the animals. Whatever he brought forth, he resolved to eat.
He eats (atti) all: that is why Aditi is called Aditi.
He who knows thus why Aditi is called Aditi becomes the eater of all this, and all becomes his food. ॥1.2.5॥
1.2.6: He desired: Let me sacrifice again, with a greater sacrifice.
From him, wearied and heated, glory and vigour went out. The prāṇas (the organs) are glory and vigour.
When the prāṇas had gone out, the body began to swell. Yet his mind was in that very body. ॥1.2.6॥
1.2.7: He desired: May this (body) of mine be fit for sacrifice, and through it may I have a body.
Then it became a horse (aśva), because it had swollen (aśvat); it had become fit for sacrifice (medhya).
That is why the horse sacrifice is called aśvamedha. He alone truly knows the aśvamedha who knows it thus.
He thought of it as let loose, unconfined.
After a year he sacrificed it to himself.

The other animals he handed over to the gods. That is why (the priests) sacrifice to Prajāpati the consecrated horse that belongs to all the gods. He who shines there (the sun) is indeed the aśvamedha; the year is his body. This fire is the arka; these worlds are its bodies. These two are the arka and the aśvamedha.
Yet they become one deity again, Death alone. (He who knows this) conquers repeated death; death does not reach him; death becomes his self; he becomes one of these deities. ॥1.2.7॥
1.3.1: Prajāpati's offspring were of two kinds: the gods and the demons.
Of them the gods were the fewer, the demons the more. They vied with one another for these worlds.
The gods said: Come, let us surpass the demons in the sacrifice by means of the udgītha, the chant of the Sāman. ॥1.3.1॥
1.3.2: They said to speech: Chant the udgītha for us.
Speech chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in speech it won for the gods by its chanting; its speaking well it kept for itself.
The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.
They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one speaks, that is the evil. ॥1.3.2॥
1.3.3: Then they said to prāṇa, the vital breath (here the breath by which one smells): Chant the udgītha for us.
Prāṇa chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in prāṇa it won for the gods by its chanting; its smelling well it kept for itself.
The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.
They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one smells, that is the evil. ॥1.3.3॥
1.3.4: Then they said to the eye: Chant the udgītha for us.
The eye said: So be it.
The eye chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the eye it won for the gods by its chanting; its seeing well it kept for itself.
The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.
They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one sees, that is the evil. ॥1.3.4॥
1.3.5: Then they said to the ear: Chant the udgītha for us.
The ear said: So be it.
The ear chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the ear it won for the gods by its chanting; its hearing well it kept for itself.
The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.
They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one hears, that is the evil. ॥1.3.5॥
1.3.6: Then they said to the mind: Chant the udgītha for us.
The mind said: So be it.
The mind chanted for them. The enjoyment that lies in the mind it won for the gods by its chanting; its thinking well it kept for itself.
The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.

They rushed at it and pierced it with evil. That evil is this: whatever unfit thing one thinks, that is the evil. So indeed they brought evils upon these deities; so they pierced them with evil. ॥1.3.6॥
1.3.7: Then they said to this prāṇa in the mouth: Chant the udgītha for us.
This prāṇa chanted for them. The demons knew: By this chanter they will surpass us.
They rushed at it and sought to pierce it with evil.
As a clod of earth would be shattered on striking a stone, so they were shattered, scattered in all directions, and perished. Then the gods came into their own, and the demons were overcome.
He who knows thus comes into his own, and the rival who hates him is overcome. ॥1.3.7॥
1.3.8: They said: Where was he who has thus joined us (to our godhood)? He is within the mouth (ayam āsye antaḥ). So he is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga). ॥1.3.8॥
1.3.9: That deity is named Dūr, for death is far (dūram) from it. Death is far from him who knows thus. ॥1.3.9॥
1.3.10: That deity took away from these deities the evil that is death, and led it to where the end of these quarters is; there it laid down their evils. Therefore one should not go to the people there, nor to that end, thinking: Let me not fall in with evil, with death. ॥1.3.10॥
1.3.11: That deity, having taken away from these deities the evil that is death, then carried them beyond death. ॥1.3.11॥
1.3.12: It carried speech beyond death first. When speech was freed from death, it became fire. This fire, having passed beyond death, blazes beyond it. ॥1.3.12॥
1.3.13: Then it carried prāṇa (the breath of smell) beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the air. This air, having passed beyond death, blows beyond it. ॥1.3.13॥
1.3.14: Then it carried the eye beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the sun. That sun, having passed beyond death, shines beyond it. ॥1.3.14॥
1.3.15: Then it carried the ear beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the quarters. These quarters have passed beyond death and are beyond it. ॥1.3.15॥
1.3.16: Then it carried the mind beyond death. When it was freed from death, it became the moon. That moon, having passed beyond death, shines beyond it. So indeed this deity carries beyond death him who knows thus. ॥1.3.16॥
1.3.17: Then it won for itself, by its chanting, the food to be eaten; for whatever food is eaten is eaten by this (prāṇa) alone, and in that food it stands firm here. ॥1.3.17॥
1.3.18: The gods said: All this is just this much, the food; and you have won it for yourself by chanting. Now give us too a share in this food.
Prāṇa said: Then enter into me from all sides.
The gods said: So be it.
They entered into it and settled all around it.

Therefore whatever food one eats by it, by that these (speech and the rest) are satisfied. So indeed do his own people gather round him who knows thus: he becomes the support of his own, their best and their leader, an eater of food (free of sickness) and their master.

But whoever among his own people wishes to be a rival to one who knows thus is not able to support his dependents; while he who follows him, or who, following him, wishes to support his dependents, he alone is able to support his dependents. ॥1.3.18॥
1.3.19: He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
Prāṇa indeed is the essence of the limbs.
Prāṇa, as all know, is the essence of the limbs; therefore from whatever limb prāṇa departs, that very limb dries up there, for it is the essence of the limbs. ॥1.3.19॥
1.3.20: He is Bṛhaspati too. Speech is bṛhatī (the Ṛk), and he is its lord (pati); therefore he is Bṛhaspati. ॥1.3.20॥
1.3.21: He is Brahmaṇaspati too. Speech is brahman (the Yajus), and he is its lord; therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati. ॥1.3.21॥
1.3.22: He is the sāman, the chant, too. Speech is sā, and this (prāṇa) is ama: sā and ama, that is why the sāman is called sāman.

Or else, because he is the same as a tiny insect (pluṣi), the same as a mosquito, the same as an elephant, the same as these three worlds, the same as this whole (universe), for that reason too he is the sāman. He who knows this sāman thus attains union with the sāman and a place in its world. ॥1.3.22॥
1.3.23: Prāṇa is ut, for by prāṇa all this is held up.
Speech alone is gīthā (song); ut and gīthā: so he is the udgītha. ॥1.3.23॥
1.3.24: On this, too, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while drinking the king (Soma), said: May this king make the head of this man (myself) fall off, if Ayāsya Āṅgirasa chanted the udgītha by any other than this (prāṇa).
For he chanted it with speech and with prāṇa alone. ॥1.3.24॥
1.3.25: He who knows the wealth (sva) of this sāman comes to have wealth.

Therefore one who is about to do the priest's work should wish for a (good) tone in his voice, and with that voice rich in tone he should do the priest's work. That is why at a sacrifice people long to see one who has a (good) tone, as they long to see one who has wealth.
Wealth comes to him who knows thus the wealth of this sāman. ॥1.3.25॥
1.3.26: He who knows the gold (suvarṇa) of this sāman comes to have gold.
Gold comes to him who knows thus the gold of this sāman. ॥1.3.26॥
1.3.27: He who knows the support (pratiṣṭhā) of this sāman stands firm.
Its support is speech alone; for it is resting on speech that this prāṇa is sung so. Some say: on food. ॥1.3.27॥
1.3.28: Now, then, the abhyāroha (the recitation of ascent), for the pavamāna hymns alone.
The prastotṛ (the priest who sings the opening) begins the sāman.

When he begins it, then (the sacrificer) should repeat these: Lead me from the untrue (asat) to the true (sat). Lead me from darkness (tamas) to light (jyotis). Lead me from death (mṛtyu) to immortality (amṛta).
When it says, Lead me from the untrue to the true, death is the untrue and immortality the true: Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal, is what it says.
Lead me from darkness to light: death is darkness and immortality is light: Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal, is what it says.

Lead me from death to immortality: here nothing is hidden, as it were. Then in the other hymns of praise (the udgātṛ) should win by chanting food to eat for himself. So in them (the sacrificer) should ask as a boon whatever wish he wishes.
This udgātṛ who knows thus wins by his chanting whatever wish he wishes, for himself or for the sacrificer.
This (knowledge) indeed wins the world. He who knows this sāman thus need never pray against being left without a world. ॥1.3.28॥
1.4.1: In the beginning this was the self (ātman) alone, in the form of a person.
Looking around, he saw nothing other than himself. He said first: I am. From that he came to be named I (aham).
That is why even now, when a man is called, he first says, It is I, and then tells whatever other name he has.
Because, being before (pūrva) all this, he burnt up (auṣat) all evils, he is puruṣa.
He who knows thus burns up him who wishes to be before him. ॥1.4.1॥
1.4.2: He was afraid; that is why one who is alone is afraid.
He reflected: Since there is nothing other than me, of what am I afraid?
At that his fear left him.
Of what should he have been afraid? It is from a second that fear arises. ॥1.4.2॥
1.4.3: He found no delight; that is why one who is alone finds no delight.
He wished for a second. He became as large as a woman and a man in close embrace.
He made this very self fall into two.
From that came husband (pati) and wife (patnī).
Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say, this (body) is one's own half, like one half of a split pea. Therefore this space is filled by the woman.
He united with her; from that, human beings were born. ॥1.4.3॥
1.4.4: She reflected: How can he unite with me, having brought me forth from himself?
She became a cow, the other a bull; he united with her, and from that cattle were born.

She became a mare, the other a stallion; she became a she-ass, the other a he-ass; he united with her, and from that the one-hoofed animals were born. She became a she-goat, the other a he-goat; she became a ewe, the other a ram; he united with her, and from that goats and sheep were born. In this way he created all that exists in pairs, down to the ants. ॥1.4.4॥
1.4.5: He knew: I myself am this creation, for it is I who created all this.
From that he came to be called creation (sṛṣṭi). He who knows thus comes to be (a creator) in this creation of his. ॥1.4.5॥
1.4.6: Then he churned thus (his hands at his mouth), and from the mouth, as from a womb, and from the hands he created fire.

Therefore both of these are hairless on the inside, for the womb is hairless on the inside. As for what they say of each god in turn, Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one: that is his manifold creation, for he himself is all the gods. And whatever is moist here he created from his seed; that is Soma.
All this is just so much: food and its eater. Soma is food; fire is its eater.

This is the higher creation (atisṛṣṭi) of Brahmā: that he created the gods, who are better than he, and that, though mortal, he created immortals. Therefore it is the higher creation. He who knows thus comes to be (a creator) in this higher creation of his. ॥1.4.6॥
1.4.7: At that time this (world) was unmanifest. It became manifest by name and form alone: this one has such a name, this one such a form.
Even now it becomes manifest by name and form alone: this one has such a name, this one such a form.

He (the Self) has entered here, up to the tips of the nails, as a razor might be laid in a razor-case, or fire (viśvambhara, the all-sustaining) in its nest (the wood). They do not see him, for (so) he is incomplete. Breathing, he is named prāṇa, the vital breath; speaking, speech; seeing, the eye; hearing, the ear; thinking, the mind: these are only the names of his acts.
Whoever worships these one by one does not know, for with each of them alone he is incomplete. One should worship him as the Self alone, for in him all these become one.
Of all this, this Self is what is to be traced, for by it one knows all this.
As one finds (a lost animal) by its footprints, so he who knows thus finds fame and the company of those dear to him. ॥1.4.7॥
1.4.8: Dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than anything else, for it is innermost: that is this Self.

If one speaks of something other than the Self as dear, (he who holds the Self dear) may say to him: What you hold dear will be cut off (will perish); he has the power to say so, and so indeed it would be. One should worship the Self alone as dear.
Whoever worships only the Self as dear: what he holds dear does not perish. ॥1.4.8॥
1.4.9: (Those who seek Brahman) say: Men think that by the knowledge of Brahman, the supreme Self, they will become all. What, then, did that Brahman know, by which it became all? ॥1.4.9॥
1.4.10: In the beginning this was Brahman alone. It knew only itself: I am Brahman.
Therefore it became all. Whoever among the gods awoke to it became that; so too among the seers, so too among men.
Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realised: I became Manu, and the sun.

And so now too, whoever knows thus, I am Brahman, becomes all this; even the gods cannot prevent his becoming so, for he becomes their Self. But whoever worships another deity, thinking, He is one being and I am another, does not know.
As a domestic animal (is to men), so is he to the gods.

Just as many animals serve a man, so each man serves the gods. Even when one animal is taken away it is unpleasant; how much more when many are. Therefore it does not please them that men should know this. ॥1.4.10॥
1.4.11: In the beginning this was the brahman (the priestly order) alone, one only.
Being one, it did not flourish. It created a better form, the kṣatra (the ruling order): those who are rulers among the gods, Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, Īśāna.
Therefore there is nothing higher than the kṣatra; therefore at the rājasūya (the royal consecration) the brāhmaṇa sits below the kṣatriya and honours him.
On the kṣatra alone he bestows that glory of his. The brahman is the source (yoni) of the kṣatra.
So, though the king attains supremacy, at the end he rests on the brahman, his own source.
Whoever harms him (the brāhmaṇa) strikes at his own source.
He becomes the more sinful, like one who harms a better man. ॥1.4.11॥
1.4.12: Still he did not flourish. He created the viś (the order of the people): those kinds of gods who are named in groups, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts. ॥1.4.12॥
1.4.13: Still he did not flourish. He created the śūdra order, Pūṣan. This (earth) is Pūṣan, for she nourishes all this, whatever there is. ॥1.4.13॥
1.4.14: Still he did not flourish. He created a better form, dharma, the law of right.

This dharma is the ruler of the ruler (the kṣatra of the kṣatra); therefore there is nothing higher than dharma. So even a weaker man hopes to prevail over a stronger one through dharma, as one does through a king.
That which is dharma is truth. Therefore of one who speaks the truth they say, He speaks dharma, and of one who speaks dharma, He speaks the truth; for both of these are this alone (dharma). ॥1.4.14॥
1.4.15: So these are the brahman, the kṣatra, the viś and the śūdra. Among the gods the brahman became (the brahman) as fire alone, among men as the brāhmaṇa; it became the kṣatriya through the kṣatriya, the vaiśya through the vaiśya, the śūdra through the śūdra. Therefore people seek a world (the fruit of their rites) among the gods in fire alone, and among men in the brāhmaṇa; for in these two forms the brahman came to be. Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world (the Self), that world, being unknown, does not protect him, any more than the Veda not recited, or any other work not done.
Even if one who does not know thus does a great holy work, it is surely exhausted for him in the end. One should worship the Self alone as one's world.
He who worships the Self alone as his world, his work is not exhausted, for out of this very Self he creates whatever he desires. ॥1.4.15॥
1.4.16: Now this self (the householder) is a world for all beings. In that he offers oblations and sacrifices, he is the world of the gods; in that he recites (the Veda), of the seers; in that he makes offerings to the ancestors and desires offspring, of the ancestors; in that he gives men shelter and gives them food, of men; in that he finds grass and water for animals, of animals; in that beasts and birds, down to the ants, live (on what is) in his houses, he is their world. As one would wish safety for one's own world (one's body), so all beings always wish safety for him who knows thus.
This has been known and has been examined. ॥1.4.16॥
1.4.17: In the beginning this was the self alone, one only.

He desired: May I have a wife; then may I be born (as offspring); then may I have wealth; then may I do work. Such indeed is the whole of desire; even wishing, one would not find more than this. That is why even now one who is alone desires: May I have a wife; then may I be born (as offspring); then may I have wealth; then may I do work.
As long as he lacks any one of these, so long he thinks himself incomplete.

The mind is his self, speech his wife, prāṇa his offspring, the eye his human wealth, for with the eye one finds it; the ear his divine wealth, for with the ear one hears it; the body (ātman) is his work, for with the body one does work.
This sacrifice is fivefold (pāṅkta); the animal is fivefold; man is fivefold; all this, whatever there is, is fivefold.
He who knows thus attains all this. ॥1.4.17॥
1.5.1: Of the seven foods that the father brought forth by intellect and austerity,
one is common to all this; two he gave the gods as their share;
for himself he made three; one he gave to the animals.
Upon it everything rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not.
Why do they not waste away, though they are eaten always?
He who knows that imperishableness eats food with his mouth (pratīka); he goes to the gods; he lives on vigour (ūrj). These are the verses. ॥1.5.1॥
1.5.2: The father brought forth the seven foods by intellect and austerity: for it was by intellect and austerity that the father brought them forth. One of them is common: this which is eaten is that common food of it.
He who worships this is not freed from evil, for it is mixed (shared by all).

Two he gave the gods as their share: what is offered into the fire (huta) and what is offered after it (prahuta). That is why people offer into the fire for the gods and make the after-offering too. Some say also that they are the new-moon and the full-moon sacrifices.
Therefore one should not be given to offering iṣṭis (sacrifices for things desired).
One he gave to the animals: that is milk.
For at first men and animals alike live on milk alone.
That is why, when a child is born, they first make it lick ghee or give it the breast to suck; and of a calf just born they say: it does not yet eat grass.
Upon it everything rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not: for it is on milk that all this rests, whatever breathes and whatever does not.

As for what they say, that one who offers milk for a year conquers recurring death (punarmṛtyu), one should not think so. On the very day he offers it, he who knows thus conquers recurring death, for he gives the gods all the food there is to eat.
Why do they not waste away, though they are eaten always: the person (puruṣa) indeed is that imperishableness, for he brings forth this food again and again.
He who knows that imperishableness: the person indeed is that imperishableness.
For he brings forth this food by thought upon thought and by his works; if he did not do so, it would waste away.
He eats food with his mouth (pratīka): pratīka is the mouth, so this means with the mouth. He goes to the gods, he lives on vigour: this is praise. ॥1.5.2॥
1.5.3: Three he made for himself: mind, speech and prāṇa, the vital breath; these he made for himself. (People say:) I was with my mind elsewhere, I did not see; I was with my mind elsewhere, I did not hear. For it is with the mind that one sees, with the mind that one hears.
Desire, conception (saṅkalpa), doubt, faith, want of faith, steadiness, unsteadiness, shame, understanding, fear: all this is mind alone.
That is why, even when touched from behind, one knows it with the mind.
Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone; for it follows an end, the thing meant, but it is not itself (a thing made known).
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna and ana: all this is prāṇa alone. This self (the body) is made of these: made of speech, made of mind, made of prāṇa. ॥1.5.3॥
1.5.4: These are the three worlds: speech is this world, mind the mid-region, prāṇa that world yonder. ॥1.5.4॥
1.5.5: These are the three Vedas: speech is the Ṛgveda, mind the Yajurveda, prāṇa the Sāmaveda. ॥1.5.5॥
1.5.6: These are the gods, the ancestors and men: speech is the gods, mind the ancestors, prāṇa men. ॥1.5.6॥
1.5.7: These are father, mother and offspring: mind is the father, speech the mother, prāṇa the offspring. ॥1.5.7॥
1.5.8: These are the known, what is sought to be known, and the unknown. Whatever is known is a form of speech, for speech is the known; speech, becoming that, protects him (who knows thus). ॥1.5.8॥
1.5.9: Whatever is sought to be known is a form of mind, for mind is what is sought to be known; mind, becoming that, protects him. ॥1.5.9॥
1.5.10: Whatever is unknown is a form of prāṇa, for prāṇa is the unknown; prāṇa, becoming that, protects him. ॥1.5.10॥
1.5.11: Of that speech the earth is the body, and this fire its luminous form. However far speech reaches, so far reaches the earth, and so far this fire. ॥1.5.11॥
1.5.12: And of this mind heaven is the body, and yonder sun its luminous form. However far mind reaches, so far reaches heaven, and so far yonder sun. The two came together in union; from that prāṇa was born.
He is Indra; he is without a rival. A second, indeed, is a rival. He who knows thus has no rival. ॥1.5.12॥
1.5.13: And of this prāṇa water is the body, and yonder moon its luminous form. However far prāṇa reaches, so far reaches water, and so far yonder moon.
These are all alike, all infinite.
He who worships them as finite wins a finite world; and he who worships them as infinite wins an infinite world. ॥1.5.13॥
1.5.14: This Prajāpati is the year, with sixteen parts (kalā). His nights (the lunar days) are fifteen parts; his sixteenth part is constant.
By the nights alone he waxes and wanes.
On the new-moon night he enters, by this sixteenth part, into all that has breath here, and then is born the next morning.
Therefore on that night one should not cut off the prāṇa of any living creature, not even of a lizard, in honour of that very deity. ॥1.5.14॥
1.5.15: That Prajāpati who is the year, with sixteen parts, is this very person who knows thus. His wealth is the fifteen parts; his self (the body) is his sixteenth part.
By wealth alone he waxes and wanes.
This self (the body) is the hub, and wealth the rim.
Therefore, even if he is stripped of everything, if he lives on in his self, people only say: he has lost his rim. ॥1.5.15॥
1.5.16: Now there are three worlds indeed: the world of men, the world of the ancestors, the world of the gods.

This world of men can be won by a son alone, by no other work; the world of the ancestors by rites, the world of the gods by knowledge. The world of the gods is the best of worlds; therefore they praise knowledge. ॥1.5.16॥
1.5.17: Now, then, the handing over (sampratti). When (a father) thinks he is about to depart, he says to his son: You are brahman (the Veda), you are the sacrifice, you are the world.
In reply the son says: I am brahman, I the sacrifice, I the world.
Of whatever has been studied, the oneness of all of it is in (the word) brahman.
Whatever sacrifices there are, the oneness of all of them is in (the word) sacrifice.
Whatever worlds there are, the oneness of all of them is in (the word) world. All this is indeed just this much. (He thinks:) This (son), being all this, will protect me from this (world).
That is why they call a son who has been taught lokya (one who wins the world for his father); that is why they teach him.
When one who knows thus departs from this world, he enters into his son together with these very prāṇas (speech, mind and prāṇa).
If anything has been left undone by him through some lapse, the son frees him from all of it.
That is why he is called a son (putra).
Through his son alone he stands firm in this world; then these divine, immortal prāṇas enter him. ॥1.5.17॥
1.5.18: Out of the earth and out of fire, divine speech enters him.
That is divine speech, by which whatever he says comes to be. ॥1.5.18॥
1.5.19: Out of heaven and out of the sun, divine mind enters him.
That is divine mind, by which he is ever joyful and does not grieve. ॥1.5.19॥
1.5.20: Out of water and out of the moon, divine prāṇa enters him.
That is divine prāṇa which, whether moving or not moving, is neither troubled nor harmed.
He who knows thus becomes the Self of all beings.
As this deity is, so is he. As all beings protect and honour this deity, so all beings protect and honour him who knows thus.
Whatever sorrow these creatures feel stays with them; only good (puṇya) goes to him. Evil does not go to the gods. ॥1.5.20॥
1.5.21: Now, then, an inquiry into the vow (vrata).
Prajāpati created the organs (karmāṇi, the instruments of acts).
Once created, they vied with one another. Speech took the vow: I will keep on speaking. The eye: I will keep on seeing. The ear: I will keep on hearing.
So did the other organs, each by its own act.
Death, becoming weariness, seized them; he reached them, and having reached them, Death held them back.

That is why speech tires, the eye tires, the ear tires. But this one he did not reach, this prāṇa in the middle. They resolved to know it: This indeed is the best of us, which, whether moving or not moving, is neither troubled nor harmed.
Come, let us all become a form of this one.
They all became a form of this one. That is why they are called by its name, prāṇas.
By the name of him who knows thus, people call the family into which he is born.
And whoever vies with one who knows thus dries up, and having dried up, dies at last. So much as regards the body (adhyātma). ॥1.5.21॥
1.5.22: Now as regards the gods (adhidaivata). Fire took the vow: I will keep on burning. The sun: I will keep on giving heat. The moon: I will keep on shining. So did the other deities, each according to its divine nature.
As the prāṇa in the middle is among these prāṇas, so is Vāyu, the wind, among these deities; for the other deities set, but not Vāyu.
Vāyu is the deity that never sets. ॥1.5.22॥
1.5.23: Now on this there is a verse: That from which the sun rises and that in which it sets — it rises from prāṇa and sets in prāṇa — that the gods made their law (dharma); it alone is today, and it tomorrow.
For what they held to then, that they do even today.
Therefore one should keep one vow alone: one should go on breathing with prāṇa and with apāna, thinking: Let evil, death, not reach me.
And if he keeps it, he should wish to carry it through. By it he attains union with this deity and a place in its world. ॥1.5.23॥
1.6.1: This (world) is indeed a triad: name, form and action.
Of these, of names, speech is their uktha (source), for from it all names arise (ut-thā).
It is their sāman, for it is equal (sama) to all names; it is their brahman, for it upholds all names. ॥1.6.1॥
1.6.2: Now of forms, the eye is their uktha, for from it all forms arise.
It is their sāman, for it is equal to all forms.
It is their brahman, for it upholds all forms. ॥1.6.2॥
1.6.3: Now of actions, the self (the body) is their uktha, for from it all actions arise; it is their sāman, for it is equal to all actions; it is their brahman, for it upholds all actions.
These three, while three, are one: this self; and the self, while one, is these three.
This is the immortal, veiled by the true (satya).
Prāṇa, the vital breath, indeed is the immortal; name and form are the true; by these two this prāṇa is veiled. ॥1.6.3॥
2.1.1: Om. There was once Dṛpta-Bālāki (the proud Bālāki) of Garga's line (Gārgya), learned in the Veda and skilled in speech.
He said to Ajātaśatru, king of Kāśī: Let me tell you of Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: For this word alone we give a thousand (cows). People run (to Janaka), saying: Janaka, Janaka. ॥2.1.1॥
2.1.2: Gārgya said: The person who is in the sun yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the one who stands above all, the head of all beings, the king.
He who worships him thus stands above all, and becomes the head of all beings, a king. ॥2.1.2॥
2.1.3: Gārgya said: The person who is in the moon yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the great one, white-robed, Soma the king.
He who worships him thus has Soma pressed for him day after day, and pressed in plenty, and his food does not fail. ॥2.1.3॥
2.1.4: Gārgya said: The person who is in the lightning yonder, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the radiant one.
He who worships him thus becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant. ॥2.1.4॥
2.1.5: Gārgya said: This person who is in space, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the full and the unmoving.
He who worships him thus is filled with offspring and cattle, and his offspring do not die out from this world. ॥2.1.5॥
2.1.6: Gārgya said: This person who is in the air, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as Indra, Vaikuṇṭha (the irresistible), the unconquered army.
He who worships him thus becomes victorious, never conquered, a conqueror of those who stand against him. ॥2.1.6॥
2.1.7: Gārgya said: This person who is in fire, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the all-withstanding (viṣāsahi).
He who worships him thus becomes all-withstanding, and his offspring become all-withstanding. ॥2.1.7॥
2.1.8: Gārgya said: This person who is in the waters, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the fitting one (pratirūpa).
He who worships him thus has what is fitting come to him, not what is unfitting, and from him is born one who is fitting. ॥2.1.8॥
2.1.9: Gārgya said: This person who is in the mirror, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the shining one.
He who worships him thus becomes shining, and his offspring become shining; and he outshines all those he comes together with. ॥2.1.9॥
2.1.10: Gārgya said: This sound that rises after a man as he walks, this alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make it a matter of talk (with me).
He who worships it thus reaches his full span of life in this world; prāṇa, the vital breath, does not leave him before his time. ॥2.1.10॥
2.1.11: Gārgya said: This person who is in the quarters, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
I worship him as the second who never departs.
He who worships him thus comes to have a companion, and his company (of his own people) is not cut off from him. ॥2.1.11॥
2.1.12: Gārgya said: This person made of shadow, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me).
He who worships him thus reaches his full span of life in this world; death does not come to him before his time. ॥2.1.12॥
2.1.13: Gārgya said: This person who is in the self, him alone I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: No, no! Do not make him a matter of talk (with me). I worship him as the self-possessed (ātmanvin).
He who worships him thus becomes self-possessed, and his offspring become self-possessed.
2.1.14: Ajātaśatru said: Is this all? Gārgya said: This is all.
Ajātaśatru said: By this much (Brahman) is not known.
Gārgya said: Let me come to you (as a pupil). ॥2.1.14॥
2.1.15: Ajātaśatru said: It goes against the natural order that a brāhmaṇa should come to a kṣatriya, thinking: He will tell me of Brahman.
Still, I shall make you know it clearly.
He took him by the hand and rose.
The two came to a man who was asleep. He called to him by these names: O great one, white-robed one, Soma, king!
He woke him by pressing him again and again with his hand.
2.1.16: Ajātaśatru said: When he was asleep thus, where was this person made of understanding (vijñānamaya) then, and from where has he come back?
2.1.17: Ajātaśatru said: When he was asleep thus,
this person made of understanding, taking by his understanding the understanding of these prāṇas (the organs), lies in the space that is within the heart.
When he takes them in, then the man is named: he sleeps (svapiti).
Then prāṇa (the sense of smell) is held in, speech is held in, the eye is held in, the ear is held in, the mind is held in. ॥2.1.17॥
2.1.18: When he moves about in dream, those are his worlds: then he becomes a great king, as it were, or a great brāhmaṇa, as it were, or goes, as it were, to states high and low.

As a great king, taking the people of his land with him, would move about as he pleases in his own country, so this one, taking the prāṇas (the organs) with him, moves about as he pleases in his own body. ॥2.1.18॥
2.1.19: Now, when he is in deep sleep, when he knows nothing whatever: there are seventy-two thousand channels called hitā, which spread out from the heart into the purītat (the membrane around the heart);
gliding back through them, he lies in the purītat.
As a young child, or a great king, or a great brāhmaṇa might lie at rest, having reached the height of bliss that wipes out all sorrow, so does this one lie. ॥2.1.19॥
2.1.20: As a spider moves up along its thread, and as tiny sparks fly out from a fire, so from this Self come forth all the prāṇas (the organs), all the worlds, all the gods, all beings. Its secret name (upaniṣad) is: the truth of the truth. The prāṇas are truth, and this is their truth. ॥2.1.20॥
2.2.1: He who knows the young one (śiśu) with its seat (ādhāna), its further seat (pratyādhāna), its post and its tether, holds back seven rivals who hate him. This young one is truly the middle prāṇa, the vital breath; this (body) is its seat, this (head) its further seat, prāṇa (strength) its post, food its tether. ॥2.2.1॥
2.2.2: These seven imperishable ones (akṣiti) attend on it: through the red streaks in the eye Rudra is bound to it; through the water in the eye, Parjanya; through the pupil, Āditya (the sun); through the black (of the eye), Agni; through the white, Indra; through the lower eyelid the earth is bound to it, through the upper, heaven.
The food of him who knows thus does not fail. ॥2.2.2॥
2.2.3: On this there is a verse:
